modules.title: Supply Chain Strategy
modules.audience: Supply chain and procurement managers, country and regional leads, finance business partners

lessons.title: 0 - Introduction
lessons.body: What this release covers, and who it is for.

lessons.title: 1 - Supply Chains, Integration and Maturity
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: A draft strategy states its objective as creating net value rather than reducing cost. What is the strongest justification for that wording?

options.text: Early leaning programmes have destroyed more value than the cost they removed
Cost data is rarely reliable across independent organisations
Only the end customer is entitled to judge what counts as value
Net value is easier to audit than a cost reduction claim

questions.text: A category manager uses supplier and vendor as interchangeable terms. Which distinction is correct?

options.text: A supplier is any seller in the market; a vendor is one the buyer has done business with
A supplier is a provider the buyer does business with; a vendor is any seller in the market
The terms differ only in whether a contract is in place for the current year
Every vendor in the market counts as one of the buyer's suppliers

questions.text: At NESR rental tools return for redress, failed components return for analysis and surplus chemicals return from the well site. What follows for network design?

options.text: Returns can be handled as exceptions by field staff at each base
Forward logistics contracts normally cover returns at no extra cost
The reverse chain carries a large share of forward value and needs the same design attention
Returns belong to disposal and can be left out of network design

questions.text: A manager argues that outsourcing freight forwarding and customs brokerage removes cost and risk with no offsetting penalty. What is actually given up?

options.text: The economies of scale a specialist provider enjoys
The lower unit prices an in-house department could achieve
Visibility of the wider process, since every interface is a place information can be lost or distorted
The legal independence of the provider, which then cannot serve competitors

questions.text: A large part of NESR inventory is maintenance, repair and operating supply. What does that class of item teach about how stock should be classified?

options.text: Value classification is sufficient, because low-value items rarely stop work
Every item should be held at every base to protect availability
Consumption is stable enough for these items to run on reorder point alone
The value of an item and the cost of its absence are different numbers, so criticality is classified alongside value

questions.text: Each function is improving itself, procurement chases lower prices, the traffic team picks better routes, and new software in one department will not exchange data with the next. Which maturity stage is that?

options.text: Multiple dysfunction, because the systems do not connect
Semifunctional enterprise, reactive but efficient inside each function
Integrated enterprise, because company-wide processes are being improved
Extended enterprise, because improvement has reached the supplier interface

questions.text: Which observation is the clearest evidence that a chain has reached the extended enterprise stage?

options.text: Enterprise-wide software running from shared, centrally accessible databases
Sales and operations planning meetings attended by every department
A logistics specialist contracted to help optimise distribution decisions
Forecasting, planning and replenishment shared and visible with a trading partner

questions.text: You are asked to place NESR on the maturity model in a way that will survive challenge. What do you do?

options.text: Assess one bounded process on observable behaviour, separately for internal and external integration
Assess the company as a whole, so the result can be compared with peers
Assess it against documented procedures, which are more objective than behaviour
Assess internal and external integration, then average the two into a single figure

lessons.title: 2 - Business Strategy
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: A supply chain strategy has been built purely as a response to the competitive strategy. Why might it still be wrong?

options.text: Business strategy is set annually while supply chain strategy runs longer
The business strategy is expressed in currency and the chain works in units
Supply chain strategy attaches to all 7 elements of the business model, not only to the competitive strategy
Only the board can approve a supply chain strategy, so it has to follow the business plan

questions.text: A colleague says the low-cost position of a service line is simply target costing applied at scale. Why is that wrong?

options.text: Target costing is a design method for hitting a cost objective; low cost is a competitive position
Target costing applies only to manufactured goods, while low cost applies to services
Target costing works back from actual cost, while low cost works forward from price
Target costing is a hybrid of low cost and focused differentiation

questions.text: A service line serves one narrowly defined customer segment, competes mainly on responsiveness, and does it at prices rivals cannot match. Which competitive position is that?

options.text: Best cost
Focused low cost
Broad differentiation
Focused differentiation

questions.text: A low-cost service line can buy a component 6% cheaper from a supplier with a higher defect rate. What is the objection?

options.text: Standardised products cannot accommodate a change of supplier
Low-cost models depend on high asset utilisation, which a new supplier disturbs
Inventory turnover will fall while the new supplier is qualified
Rework and returns cut deeply into the thin margins a low-cost model runs on

questions.text: An operation competing on responsiveness must choose between substantial safety stock and investment in supply chain agility. Why is that choice often made badly?

options.text: Agility always costs more in total than safety stock over the life of a product
Safety stock cost never appears in the accounts, so it is left out of the comparison
Agility is expensive to set up and cheap to run while safety stock is the reverse, so the option that is cheaper this quarter wins
Placing warehouses nearer to users is ruled out in any low-cost model

questions.text: In a strategy built on innovation, why does time to volume matter as much as time to market?

options.text: Volume production lowers unit cost enough to fund the next development
Regulators require demonstrated volume before wide marketing is permitted
Early adopters pay a premium only once volume is available
Demand peaks early in the release and then falls away, so demand missed in that window damages profit badly

questions.text: A carrier competing purely on price obviously still needs safe aircraft. What does that tell you about the role of safety in its strategy?

options.text: Safety is a second basis of competition running alongside low cost
Safety is a constraint the model has to satisfy, not the basis on which it competes
A low-cost model has to accept lower standards on attributes customers do not pay for
The position is really best cost, because both cost and quality are in play

questions.text: A client asks a low-cost service line for a guaranteed 24-hour response. What is the right response from supply chain?

options.text: Name the trade-off and price it, so the decision is made explicitly
Absorb it, because the client relationship outweighs one service change
Refuse it, because it contradicts the chosen basis of competition
Accept it and recover the cost at the next contract renewal

lessons.title: 3 - Organizational Strategy
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: A lateral chain contains many independent firms, each with its own goals and systems. Whose strategy does supply chain strategy align with?

options.text: The largest supplier's, because upstream constraints govern the chain
The channel master's, traditionally the manufacturer at the centre or a dominant retailer
A weighted average of all partners' strategies, in proportion to spend
The end customer's stated preferences, since the customer funds the chain

questions.text: A redesign raises total chain profit but leaves one critical supplier earning below its cost of capital. How should that be judged?

options.text: Acceptable, because total chain profitability is the measure that matters
Acceptable, provided the supplier is not the channel master
A pricing problem for that supplier to solve at its next negotiation
Not aligned, because the chain will fail at that link at the worst possible moment

questions.text: A warehouse is measured on cost per pallet and the service line it feeds is measured on rig-site availability. What has been created?

options.text: A designed disagreement that staff are then asked to resolve informally
A healthy tension that keeps both cost and service under review
A gap in the metrics, since neither measure covers total cost
An alignment problem only the channel master can settle

questions.text: Field warehouses decide their own replenishment, and material is issued only when the using operation signals for it. What kind of system is that?

options.text: A push system, because the warehouses hold stock ahead of orders
A push system, because replenishment decisions stay local
A pull system, in which withdrawal by the user triggers replacement
A hybrid, because issuing to a signal is a scheduling rule rather than a pull rule

questions.text: A manager claims that becoming demand-driven removes the need for forecasting. What is the correct answer?

options.text: Correct, because a strictly demand-driven chain has no fixed production schedule
Correct, because point-of-sale data replaces the forecast at every stage
Wrong, because the push-pull frontier cannot move past the distribution centre
Wrong, because forecasts still drive raw material delivery on the supplier side of the plant

questions.text: Which statement correctly describes the risk traded when a chain moves from forecast-push to demand-pull?

options.text: Push risks inventory build-up and obsolescence; pull risks orders arriving above capacity and expensive recovery
Pull removes stockout risk, because product is made only against confirmed orders
Push removes stockout risk, because safety stock accumulates at every stage
Pull removes obsolescence and capacity risk together, which is why it is the safer choice

questions.text: A product line shows forecast error of 40% to 100%, a life cycle of about 3 months and contribution margins of 20% to 60%. Which chain design fits it?

options.text: High average utilisation, minimal inventory with high turns, suppliers chosen on cost and quality
Short lead time consistent with low cost, and design for maximum performance at minimum cost
Buffer capacity and safety stock, aggressive lead-time reduction, suppliers chosen for agility
Small stocked quantities moved in full loads on steady year-round replenishment

questions.text: Replacement parts for customised equipment have predictable low-margin demand but lead times of 6 to 12 months. How should they be treated?

options.text: As innovative items, because the long lead time demands buffer capacity
As functional items served by a predictable low-cost chain that accepts a long make-to-order lead time
As fashion items, because demand arrives in unpredictable bursts
As seasonal items, because demand follows the maintenance calendar

lessons.title: 4 - The Business Model
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: Tactical functional plans are stated in units while the business plan is stated in currency, and they do not agree. Where does that disagreement usually appear first?

options.text: In the year-end financial statements, as an unexplained cost variance
In the revenue model, as a margin shortfall by channel
As a capacity argument inside sales and operations planning, which is a symptom rather than the cause
In the asset footprint, as an unplanned facility requirement

questions.text: Why must customer service, sales channels, the value system, the operating model and the asset footprint be planned together?

options.text: Because they are the five forces that determine industry profitability
Because customer service cannot be measured without sales channel data
Because the business plan is stated in currency and tactical plans in units
Because deciding them in isolation produces suboptimisation and conflicting goals

questions.text: Which decision is the primary source of an organisation's costs?

options.text: What to own, where and at what scale
Labour rates in the chosen production geographies
Freight rates negotiated with carriers
The service level promised in customer contracts

questions.text: On what basis can an in-house warehouse be said to add value?

options.text: Its cost per pallet has fallen year on year
It meets the service levels set out in the business plan
It does the job better, faster or more cheaply than competitors and third-party providers would
Every activity inside it has been mapped and classified as value-adding

questions.text: A base claims its in-house tool-tracking system is a core capability, because a competitor would find it cost-prohibitive to develop or licence. Which area of competitive advantage is that?

options.text: Economies of scale
Technology
Geographic expertise and capacity
Resources such as materials and financing

questions.text: An item has sporadic demand and a wide variety of configurations. Which operating model fits, and what cost profile comes with it?

options.text: Make-to-stock, with low production cost and high inventory carrying cost
Make-to-order, with high production cost but low inventory carrying and planning cost
Assemble-to-order, with moderate production cost and low carrying cost
Engineer-to-order, with costs initiated only after payment is agreed

questions.text: A product needs highly specialised expertise and heavy capital investment, and management wants the lowest unit production cost. Which asset footprint, and what does it cost you?

options.text: Global, with one set of locations, which requires spending to address business interruption risk
Regional, with production localised by region to cut transport time
Country-specific, to avoid duties and satisfy local sourcing rules
Regional, with cross-swapping of products between regions

questions.text: A critical tool is short and three jobs want it. Where does that decision properly belong?

options.text: With the duty planner, applying available-to-promise at the moment of shortage
With the client holding the steepest penalty clause, as a standing rule
With the operating model, since it governs delivery lead times
With the revenue model, as an allocation policy decided in advance

lessons.title: 5 - External Inputs
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: A planning team lists newly announced import regulations among the variables it intends to manage. What is wrong with that?

options.text: Regulations belong to the competition part of a scan rather than the market conditions part
These are external forces that can be understood but not controlled, so they are inputs rather than variables
Regulatory change is too slow to affect a supply chain strategy
Only the legal function is permitted to hold regulatory items in a plan

questions.text: What should an environmental scan actually produce?

options.text: A more accurate demand forecast for the coming planning horizon
A ranked list of external forces the organisation can influence
A long-range plan robust enough to survive an economic shock
A strategy flexible enough to adopt a new direction quickly when conditions change

questions.text: Frequent power cuts in several African markets left demand unmet, and a manufacturer built a freezer that keeps food frozen for 100 hours without electricity. Which scanning activity found that?

options.text: Scanning market conditions for the impact of recent events and disasters
Scanning global forces for rising project complexity
Scanning the competition, including customer requirements going unsatisfied
Benchmarking supply chain maturity against comparable organisations

questions.text: A downturn is treated as a chance to take significant share from an established competitor. What has to be true for that to work?

options.text: Customer requirements are satisfied either more completely or at lower cost than rivals manage
Prices are cut below the market until weaker rivals withdraw
Capital investment is deferred until leading indicators turn positive
The business withdraws from regions where it does not already hold most of the share

questions.text: A benchmarking exercise reports that the company's own chain is world class. What warning applies to that conclusion?

options.text: Benchmarking cannot compare across industries, so the result is not meaningful
Benchmarking measures cost only, so service performance stays unproven
The result becomes valid only once every region uses the same measures
What an organisation believes is world class may already have been surpassed

questions.text: Sourcing and manufacturing have spread across more countries and time zones. What does that force specifically demand?

options.text: Flexibility and agility designed in ahead of the volatility
Project management discipline supported by systems rather than spreadsheets
More formal mechanisms for coordination and collaboration
Greater reliance on informal coordination between regional teams

questions.text: Supply chain projects now run with large teams at remote sites and volumes of information that cannot be handled manually at the speed required. What does that demand?

options.text: Genuine project management discipline, supported by systems rather than spreadsheets
More formal mechanisms for coordination between trading partners
Flexibility and agility designed in ahead of the volatility
Local managers and experts attuned to regional differences

questions.text: Every region reports its performance in its own terms, and the reports cannot be compared. What practice fixes that?

options.text: Require each region to explain variances against its own prior year
Track every region on the same standard measures, such as flexibility, velocity and predictability
Consolidate reporting into a single global figure for each measure
Have each region benchmark itself against a local competitor

lessons.title: 6 - Strategy Objectives and the Three Vs
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

quiz.title: Strategy Objectives and the Three Vs

questions.text: A partner will not share account information, so the team buys consumer data from a survey company instead. What is that purchased data actually good for?

options.text: Replacing the partner's transaction records for relationship management
Establishing which of the partner's customers are unprofitable
Acquiring new customers, rather than managing the ones already held
Setting service levels for the accounts the partner holds

questions.text: Two years into a collaboration a partner still will not share customer account information. How should that be read?

options.text: As a normal stage of implementation, since trust has to build before account data is shared
As evidence the collaboration has failed and should be replaced
As a signal to buy the equivalent data and stop asking
As grounds to escalate through the contract

questions.text: Why is visibility described as a working capital lever rather than a reporting improvement?

options.text: Because dashboards cost less than the reporting they replace
Because better visibility raises velocity, and higher velocity permits less safety stock
Because visibility is itself measured in days of inventory
Because shared data allows partners to fund inventory jointly

questions.text: Point-of-sale data is visible at the same moment to warehouse, plant and supplier systems. Where does the saving come from?

options.text: The improved accuracy of the forecast built on that data
The reporting staff the automation makes unnecessary
The lower cost of holding data centrally rather than locally
Actions triggered automatically, without waiting for someone to read a report and pass it on

questions.text: Faster transport modes are one way to raise velocity. What qualification applies?

options.text: Only for goods at risk of damage or spoiling while at rest
Only after all non-value-added activities have been eliminated
Only where there is a net benefit once the higher transport cost is counted
Only where the customer has agreed to fund the premium

questions.text: How does supply variability behave along a chain?

options.text: It increases in waves downstream, smallest at extraction and largest at the retail end
It increases upstream, smallest at retail and largest at extraction
It stays roughly constant, because suppliers hold buffer capacity
It cannot be reduced at all, unlike demand variability

questions.text: A distributor's orders have followed a steady pattern for 6 months, and the planner treats the pattern as reliable. Which practice guards against the bullwhip effect here?

options.text: Holding additional safety stock until the pattern is proven
Widening the product variety offered to that distributor
Increasing order frequency to smooth the pattern
Deliberate communication with the distributor rather than reading order history as intent

questions.text: Beyond avoiding losses, what does planning for risk in advance buy an organisation?

options.text: Lower insurance premiums, justified by documented contingency plans
Shared risk with prepared partners, and a workforce confident to act on substantiated data
A permanently reduced need for safety stock across the chain
Formal credit under sustainability reporting

lessons.title: 7 - Value and the Value Chain
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: Where does the alignment of supply chain strategy with organisational strategy have to start?

options.text: By identifying customers, products, competition and the socioeconomic environment, then setting mission and goals
By setting the competitive priorities of cost, quality, time and price
By defining the functional strategies for finance, marketing and supply chain
By listing the supply chain capabilities available now and in the long term

questions.text: Which statement matches a value stream?

options.text: A string of collaborating players working together to satisfy market demand
The functions inside one company that add value to what it sells
The processes of creating, producing and delivering a good or service, including timing
The network of entities through which cash flows back upstream

questions.text: A sensible supply chain initiative stalls inside legal and human resources. What is the usual reason?

options.text: Deliberate obstruction by functions protecting their budgets
Absence of executive sponsorship for cross-functional work
Those functions sit outside the value chain entirely
Those managers cannot distinguish a value chain from a supply chain, so they do not know what is required of them

questions.text: A warehouse is closed to save storage cost, and transport cost then rises by more than the saving. How should that be classified?

options.text: A justified saving, since storage is a non-value-added activity
Cost moving rather than cost cutting, because there is no net gain at the customer's end
An acceptable trade-off, since the two costs sit in different budgets
Sound practice, because warehousing and transport were considered together

questions.text: Automated handling equipment costs USD 1,200,000 and is expected to save USD 260,000 a year for 6 years. On the test applied to supply chain investment, what is the verdict?

options.text: Justified, because savings of USD 1,560,000 exceed the investment
Not justified, because the annual saving is less than a quarter of the investment
Not justified, because the payback runs beyond 4 years
Justified only if the equipment also raises customer satisfaction

questions.text: A nucleus firm keeps the whole benefit of a joint improvement and leaves its suppliers carrying the cost of the change. What is the likely outcome?

options.text: Suppliers absorb it, since the nucleus firm controls the volume
The saving is recovered later through higher prices to the end customer
The best suppliers leave first, because they are the ones with somewhere better to go
The chain becomes more efficient, since weak suppliers are driven out

questions.text: A customer does not value immediate availability and the product does not require it, yet air freight is used routinely. How should that be judged?

options.text: Justified, since availability is one of the values customers hold
Justified, provided the freight cost is offset by cuts elsewhere
Neutral, because effectiveness outweighs efficiency in customer-facing decisions
Not a rational decision, but a habit with a freight invoice attached

questions.text: An activity raises value for one partner and reduces it for another. What is the test of whether the arrangement can stand?

options.text: Whether total value across the chain has increased
Whether every party stays satisfied enough to keep participating
Whether the nucleus firm has approved the redistribution
Whether the end customer sees a lower price

lessons.title: 8 - Capabilities and Customer Service
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: A business unit earns a net margin of 3% on revenue of USD 400 million, and its supply chain costs are USD 160 million. What does a 5% cut in supply chain cost do to net income?

options.text: Raises it from USD 12 million to USD 20 million, an increase of about 67%
Raises it from USD 12 million to USD 12.6 million, an increase of 5%
Raises it from USD 12 million to USD 28 million, an increase of about 133%
Raises it by USD 8 million, which is an increase of about 8%

questions.text: What is an enterprise resources planning system at its core?

options.text: A planning engine that converts forecasts into production schedules
An accounting-oriented database that coordinates information flow across the organisation and its partners
A network of intranets and extranets linking trading partners
A measurement system that compares performance against external standards

questions.text: A manager reports that the cash-to-cash cycle has fallen from 50 days to 20 days, and that this is better than the industry average. Which measurement standards is that using?

options.text: Desired future performance and world-class performance
A named competitor's performance and the industry average
Desired future performance and the industry average
Past performance and the industry average

questions.text: The obstacles to supply chain technology are rarely technical. What is the most significant challenge?

options.text: The cost of licences and implementation
New users questioning whether the system is useful
Lack of trust between companies, and between functions, about sharing data
The absence of integrated intranets and extranets

questions.text: Before an organisation can leverage a partner's strengths, what has to happen?

options.text: The strengths have to be identified and named
The partnership has to be formalised as a joint legal entity
The partner's costs have to be opened for inspection
Both organisations have to adopt a common technology platform

questions.text: Of 500 customer orders shipped last month, 40 went out missing at least one line item. What does the orders-shipped-complete measure record?

options.text: 96%, since only the missing lines count as failures
98%, since most items on those orders were delivered
92%, because an order missing any item at all is counted as incomplete
It cannot be calculated without knowing the total number of line items

questions.text: One manager calls an air freight shipment wasteful and another calls it necessary. What is going on?

options.text: One holds total cost data and the other does not
One is measuring efficiency and the other effectiveness, so both can be right
The disagreement is about the customer service strategy rather than the shipment
Air freight is efficient but not effective, so the first manager is right

questions.text: An organisation competes on low cost. What should its supply chain be prepared to give up?

options.text: Economies of scale, which need capital the model will not fund
Use of third parties, since margins cannot cover their fees
Measurement of asset utilisation, which matters only in premium models
Responsiveness such as guaranteed emergency delivery, because responsiveness correlates with cost

lessons.title: 9 - Optimisation
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: A chain has removed every buffer and pared every process time to the minimum. What is the strategic exposure?

options.text: Suppliers will raise prices once they see the buffers have gone
Quality will fall because inspection time has been removed
Complexity will rise as exceptions are handled manually
It has lost the flexibility to change direction, and can run efficiently towards a market that is no longer there

questions.text: A company with automated workflows and cross-company networks was left holding more than USD 2 billion of useless inventory when demand for its products collapsed. What was the cause?

options.text: The networks failed technically during the demand collapse
Its outsourced suppliers never got word that demand was vanishing and kept shipping into inventory
It had brought manufacturing back in house and could not cut output quickly
It was demand-driven, so it had no forecast to warn it

questions.text: Consumers moved online fast enough to drive e-commerce growth of 70% a year for 4 years, and established consumer goods firms were left with stock their physical stores could not sell. Which factor forced a strategy change?

options.text: A change in market conditions
A disruptive technology entering the industry
An anticipated change in the market
A business combination or merger

questions.text: A manufacturer launched a vehicle with no comparable predecessor and no demand history to forecast from. What did it do?

options.text: Allocated cars to dealers on past performance, to spread the risk
Built to a fixed schedule and discounted whatever was left over
Shipped to central distribution centres and released to dealers only against customer orders, accepting a costlier network for the flexibility
Delayed the launch until leading indicators confirmed regional demand

questions.text: Before asking for data on strategy gaps, why ask whether the culture punishes failure?

options.text: Because data collection is prohibitively expensive in a punitive culture
Because gaps are usually noticed but not reported, and only a safe culture produces the critics who report them
Because outside consultants cannot work where failure is punished
Because anonymous surveys are invalid unless the culture is already open

questions.text: A workshop asks every participant for 5 reasons a proposed strategy might fail. Why is it framed that way?

options.text: It makes participation the safe option, where asking whether it might fail invites a show of loyalty
It produces a longer list than open discussion would
It allows the reasons to be ranked statistically afterwards
It prevents any single participant from dominating the session

questions.text: Which lever reduces supply chain complexity without damaging flexibility?

options.text: Reduce the asset footprint used for production and distribution
Reduce the number of distinct supply chains maintained
Move configuration to a later stage in the process
Limit the range of products and services offered

questions.text: Your organisation is the channel master and has spent years pressing partners for price concessions. What should you expect when you now ask them to align with a new strategy?

options.text: Rapid compliance, since the commercial relationship is already established
Alignment on price terms but not on information sharing
Quiet resistance, and influence is better used to promote collaboration than control
A demand to renegotiate contracts before any change is discussed

lessons.title: 10 - Economics for Supply Chain Strategy
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: A manager argues that growth of 3% in gross domestic product means a NESR product line will grow 3%. What is wrong with the reasoning?

options.text: Gross domestic product is a lagging indicator and arrives too late to plan with
Real gross domestic product excludes services, which is most of the line
Aggregate data describes all goods in an economy and cannot be applied directly to one company's products
Growth in gross domestic product affects aggregate supply rather than aggregate demand

questions.text: You need the earliest possible signal that consumer demand is about to change. Which index, and why?

options.text: The consumer confidence index, because it reports intentions and so leads demand
The consumer price index, because prices move before volumes
The producer price index, because producers see orders first
Real gross domestic product, because it is the broadest measure available

questions.text: Your prices fall 4% over a year while competitors' prices fall 9%. What has effectively happened to your position?

options.text: A price reduction of 4%, which should raise volume
The equivalent of a price increase, because demand responds to relative prices
No change, because both moved in the same direction
A margin problem alone, since customers see a lower price than last year

questions.text: A price cut of 8% is followed by a rise in total revenue of 5%. What does the total revenue test tell you?

options.text: Demand is inelastic, because revenue moved by less than price
Demand is inelastic, because the price cut was not fully recovered
Nothing, until the elasticity coefficient has been calculated
Demand is elastic, because the extra volume more than replaced the revenue given up

questions.text: Price falls from USD 130 to USD 120 and demand rises from 260 units to 340 units. What is the price elasticity coefficient?
A consumable costs USD 60 a unit to supply. At a price of USD 120 demand is 340 units; at USD 100 it is 460 units. On gross margin, which price wins and by how much?

options.text: USD 120, by USD 2,000
USD 100, by USD 2,000
USD 100, by USD 18,400
The two prices produce the same gross margin

questions.text: A consumable costs USD 60 a unit. Logistics cost is USD 5 a unit at 260 units, USD 12 at 340 units and USD 18 at 400 units, at prices of USD 130, USD 120 and USD 110. Which price wins?

options.text: USD 120, at USD 16,320
USD 130, at USD 16,900
USD 110, at USD 12,800
USD 120, at USD 20,400

questions.text: A scheduled run costs USD 1,400 and carries 12,000 kg. A backload of 3,000 kg is offered at USD 0.06 per kg. Extra fuel is USD 24, the detour USD 46 and handling USD 35. What follows?

options.text: Refuse, because USD 0.06 a kg is below the average cost of about USD 0.12
Refuse, because the vehicle lease and depot overhead are not covered
Accept, but only if the offer is raised to the average cost per kg
Accept, because the offer of USD 180 exceeds the marginal cost of USD 105

lessons.title: 11 - Financial Statements
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: Standard usage is 3 kg per unit at USD 20 per kg, and 500 units were produced. Actual consumption was 1,650 kg at USD 19 per kg. What are the usage and rate variances?

options.text: Usage minus USD 3,000 and rate minus USD 1,650
Usage minus USD 1,350 and rate plus USD 1,650
Usage minus USD 3,000 and rate plus USD 1,650
Usage plus USD 1,650 and rate minus USD 3,000

questions.text: A material cost variance recurs every month through a period of volatile input prices. What should be considered before treating it as a performance failure?

options.text: That the cost driver used to allocate overhead has been chosen wrongly
That cost accounting is forward-looking and so unsuitable for control
That usage and rate variances should be combined into one reported figure
That the standard itself may need revising, perhaps quarterly or even monthly

questions.text: A base expects overhead of USD 600,000 for the period across 15,000 direct labour hours for all its operations. A single operation is expected to take 900 hours. What is its standard overhead cost?
A period closes with a total overhead variance of zero, made up of a usage variance of minus USD 9,400 and a rate variance of plus USD 9,400. What should be reported?

options.text: The zero total, since the components cancel and no action is available
Both components, because the usage overrun is controllable while the rate largely is not
The rate variance alone, because it is the favourable figure
The zero total, with a note that standards may need revising

questions.text: Why is depreciation added back when a statement of cash flows is prepared by the indirect method?

options.text: Because the tax benefit it provides increases the cash received
Because reporting rules require non-cash charges to be disclosed separately
Because it reduces net income without reducing cash, so it has to be reversed to reach cash flow
Because it belongs in the investing section rather than the operating section

questions.text: A unit reports revenue of USD 240 million, cost of goods sold of USD 156 million and net income of USD 16 million. What are its margins, and what does that shape imply?

options.text: 35% and 6.67%, so cost of goods sold has little effect on net income
65% and 6.67%, so the unit is unusually profitable for a services business
35% and 10%, so the margin is comfortable enough to absorb cost increases
35% and 6.67%, so a movement of 1% in cost of goods sold moves net income by roughly 15%

questions.text: A unit holds inventory of USD 39 million against cost of goods sold of USD 156 million, receivables of USD 60 million on revenue of USD 240 million, and payables of USD 26 million. What is its cash-to-cash cycle?

options.text: About 122 days
About 61 days
About 183 days
About 31 days

questions.text: Raising inventory turns from 4.0 to 5.0 releases USD 7.8 million of cash. Taking 15 days off receivables of 91 days releases USD 9.9 million. Which lever, and what is supply chain's part in it?

options.text: Inventory, because the cash it releases is permanent while collections is a one-off
Collections, and supply chain owns the delivery proof behind most disputed invoices
Inventory, because collections belongs to finance
Either, since the amounts are close enough to make it an operational preference

lessons.title: 12 - Strategic Analysis Tools
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: A hardware company let an outside developer keep the rights to an operating system, because software was not its business. What lesson does that carry for strategic analysis?

options.text: An opportunity that is ignored or poorly developed turns into a threat
Opportunities outside current core capabilities should always be declined
Threats can be converted into opportunities by licensing them out
Strengths and opportunities belong in the same quadrant of the analysis

questions.text: Why should the weaknesses in a strategic analysis be evidenced from customers and suppliers rather than internally?

options.text: External parties assess strengths more objectively as well
An internal list contains only the weaknesses the organisation is already comfortable admitting
Internal data on skills and facilities is usually out of date
Weaknesses belong on the external side of the analysis

questions.text: A team puts a newly announced import tariff on drilling consumables into the weaknesses quadrant. Where does it belong?

options.text: Weaknesses, because it raises the organisation's landed cost
Strengths, if competitors are more exposed to it than you are
Threats, because it is external, negative and outside the organisation's control
Opportunities, because tariffs can be mitigated by local sourcing

questions.text: A study compares the company's share of current market demand with rivals' shares over 3 years. Which type of market research is that?

options.text: Consumer research
Market analysis
Environmental scanning
Sales analysis

questions.text: Assembling in Asia saves USD 18 per unit in labour. Duty on the finished product is USD 26 a unit against USD 9 on components, and inbound freight on parts is USD 7 a unit lower. Where do you assemble?

options.text: Asia, by USD 18 a unit
Europe, by USD 6 a unit
Europe, by USD 24 a unit
Asia, by USD 11 a unit

questions.text: When is a network model of a supply chain complex enough?

options.text: When it reproduces the chain realistically at every node
When it has been validated against a full year of history
When it includes every cost that appears in the income statement
When it can reliably help decision makers choose between the available options

questions.text: A target raises order fill rate from 93% to 98%, and the base ships 4,000 order lines a month. What does the target require, and what does a balanced measurement framework add?

options.text: 40 more lines filled a month, and a single measure that replaces the others
500 more lines filled a month, and a direct comparison against competitors
200 more lines filled a month, and a comprehensive view of performance rather than a single isolated measure
200 more lines filled a month, and an audited basis for reporting to investors

questions.text: A network model built in a spreadsheet has not been independently checked. What is the risk?

options.text: A model with an error in it is more dangerous than no model, because it comes with a number attached
Spreadsheets cannot run simulation techniques reliably
Spreadsheet models cannot be used for facility location work
The model will be too simple to represent the chain

lessons.title: 13 - Wrap-up
lessons.body: A recap of the release, and what it sets you up to do next.

modules.title: Supply Chain and Product Design
modules.audience: Network and design owners, engineering and product interfaces, anyone building a business case

lessons.title: 0 - Introduction
lessons.body: What this release covers, and who it is for.

lessons.title: 1 - Market Research for Design
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: You are sizing capacity against a demand forecast prepared by the commercial team. Which bias should you expect that forecast to carry, and what makes it worse?

options.text: Optimism, magnified because senior management seldom looks favourably on cautious estimates
Pessimism, magnified because marketing protects itself against missed targets
Optimism, magnified because sales commission is paid on forecast accuracy
Pessimism, magnified because engineering overstates technical risk

questions.text: On most tenders, health and safety performance and technical compliance are order qualifiers. What follows for where money is spent?

options.text: Investment in qualifiers should stop, because they do not win orders
Spending to lift a qualifier above the threshold buys nothing, because it does not differentiate
Qualifiers should be promoted hardest, because customers notice them first
Qualifiers become winners once performance exceeds every competitor

questions.text: A documentation failure delays a customs clearance and the client awards the next job elsewhere. Which competitive characteristic does that describe?

options.text: An order winner, because paperwork quality differentiates the firm
An order qualifier, because compliance is a threshold requirement
An order loser, because poor performance in that area causes business to be lost
Demand generation, because it changes the customer's buying behaviour

questions.text: A new downhole tool is being launched. Who does the demand generation campaign actually have to convince?

options.text: The rig crew who will physically operate the tool on site
The wider public, so that brand awareness supports the sales force
The client's procurement department alone, since it signs the order
The drilling engineer, the company man, the category manager and the technical authority

questions.text: Which contribution of market research to product design is most often left out altogether?

options.text: Support needs, documentation languages, return policy and attitudes to disposal
Dividing the market into segments using who, where, when and why
Quantifying an unmet need the sales force has already reported
Identifying which features contribute positively to the profit margin

questions.text: How do marketing and sales differ in the direction they translate information?

options.text: Marketing translates the internal perspective outward and sales translates the external perspective inward
Both translate the external perspective for internal audiences, differing only in detail
Marketing translates the external perspective for internal audiences; sales translates the internal perspective for external audiences
Marketing sets price and sales sets volume, so neither translates information

questions.text: Research shows one segment wants a heavy-duty housing and another wants the lightest possible unit. Neither variant improves the profit margin. What should the research input to design become?

options.text: Build both variants and let sales volume decide which one survives
Identify the most profitable segments instead of pursuing the variation
Adopt the variant preferred by the larger segment and drop the other
Defer the decision until the product reaches its growth stage

questions.text: A launch campaign succeeds and creates more demand than the chain can serve. Why is that worse than not launching at all?

options.text: Because promotional spending cannot be recovered once committed
Because the product then has to be repriced below its planned margin
Because latent demand can never be converted a second time by any campaign
Because it spends credibility as well as money, turning away exactly the buyers the campaign created

lessons.title: 2 - The Four Ps and Demand Shaping
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

quiz.title: The Four Ps and Demand Shaping

questions.text: Why is demand shaping a supply chain tool rather than purely a marketing one?

options.text: Because it lowers promotional cost, which is charged to distribution
Because it influences demand so that demand better matches available supply
Because it replaces forecasting with firm customer orders
Because it transfers pricing authority to the logistics function

questions.text: A business moves from one product, one price, one channel and one message to a customer-focused model. What does that shift hand to the supply chain?

options.text: A reduction in complexity, because segments buy more predictably
More configurations to hold, pricing complexity in order-to-cash, and channels with different fulfilment economics
No material consequence for fulfilment, since it is a marketing change
A case for abandoning segmentation as unaffordable

questions.text: A rig location has no lay-down space and no crew to receive goods until its scheduled slot. Which delivery characteristic is worth most there?

options.text: Overnight delivery, because speed always reduces exposure
The lowest freight rate, since transport is a controllable cost
Consistent delivery that is neither early nor late
High-touch counter service, which can command a premium price

questions.text: A channel is judged accessible, convenient, fast and flexible by customers, while the business wants control, consistency and profitability. What is the relationship between those two sets of criteria?

options.text: They pull against each other, because convenience and speed usually need more human resource
They align, because satisfied customers cost less to serve over time
Both can be maximised once the channel is digital
They apply to different channels and should never be compared

questions.text: Customers increasingly transfer loyalty from the product to the provider who keeps it available. Why is that a supply chain statement?

options.text: Because brand spending should be cut and reinvested in stock
Because packaging design becomes the main driver of repeat purchase
Because responsibility for brand image moves to the promotion budget
Because if loyalty attaches to availability and recovery, then availability and recovery are the brand

questions.text: A generic lamp made on the same line as a branded one sells worse at its lower price. What does that show about price and demand?

options.text: Demand always falls as price falls once a brand is involved
Price has no effect on demand in commodity markets
Demand generally rises as price falls, but a higher price can add status appeal and raise perceived value
Demand is fixed by the product design, so pricing is irrelevant

questions.text: Which pricing task is named as the natural point for supply chain collaboration with the commercial team?

options.text: Setting the annual margin target for each segment
Choosing which customers receive fee waivers
Deciding the discount tier granted to the largest accounts
Synchronising the selling price with the costs of design, manufacturing and logistics

questions.text: A printer cartridge is sold in a box designed to be reused for returning the spent unit. Which purposes does that single package serve?

options.text: Marketing appeal, reverse logistics and reduced environmental impact together
Marketing appeal only, since the return is a separate service decision
Reverse logistics only, because a functional box cannot also sell the product
Freight cost reduction only, since returns are handled by the carrier

lessons.title: 3 - Financial Modelling
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: Which costs and benefits belong in the financial model for a decision to create or improve part of a supply chain?

options.text: Marginal ones: the increase in cost and the increase in benefit
Total costs and total revenues for the whole business unit
Capital costs only, since operating costs recur regardless
Intangible benefits only, since tangible ones are already budgeted

questions.text: Interest rates are 10% a year. What is the present value of USD 100 to be received a year from now?
A hub costs USD 2,400,000 and returns USD 700,000 a year for 5 years. Discounted at 10%, the inflows have a total present value of USD 2,653,551. What is the net present value?
The same hub shows a simple payback of 3.43 years and a discounted payback of 4.42 years, and the site is held on a 5-year lease. What does the discounted figure tell the approver?

options.text: The investment fails to pay back within the lease and should be refused
It clears the lease by about 7 months rather than by more than 18 months
The two measures agree, so either one supports the same decision
Discounted payback is irrelevant once net present value is positive

questions.text: An investment of USD 2,400,000 produces a net operating cash inflow of USD 700,000 in year 1, and the cost of capital is 10%. What is the economic value added in year 1?

An investment of USD 1,800,000 returns USD 500,000 a year. At a 10% discount rate the cumulative present value after year 4 is USD 1,584,900, and year 5 contributes USD 310,450. What is the discounted payback period?

options.text: 3.60 years
4.31 years
4.69 years
5.40 years

questions.text: A product is expected to become obsolete quickly. What does that imply for the payback the supporting investment must achieve?

options.text: A longer payback is acceptable, because obsolescence lowers the discount rate
Payback becomes irrelevant, because net present value settles the case
A 6-year payback is the accepted threshold for any capital project
It needs a fast payback, or the capital must have an alternative use afterwards

questions.text: What does economic value added show that return on investment, as normally presented, does not?

options.text: It discounts every future cash flow to present value
It states the break-even point in years
It separates tangible benefits from intangible ones
It charges the cost of the capital invested before profit is calculated

lessons.title: 4 - Translating Strategy Into Design
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: A team proposes expensive hardware and software to speed up order processing immediately upstream of a known bottleneck. What is the correct assessment?

options.text: It increases queue rather than throughput, so the spend achieves nothing
It is justified, because faster information always improves customer service
It is justified provided the payback period is under 3 years
It removes the bottleneck by making the constraint visible sooner

questions.text: A design document covers partners, facility locations and capacity, products, and transport modes. Against the definition of supply chain design, what is missing?

options.text: The organisational strategy statement
The supporting information systems
The metrics and key performance indicators
The discount rate used in the financial model

questions.text: Why is it more realistic to say that design decisions and strategy should be consistent, rather than that every decision follows from strategy?

options.text: Because supply chain strategy is written after the network is built
Because operational managers rarely read the strategy document
Because it is a chicken and egg question: design reveals what is possible and strategy adjusts to it
Because there is one universally correct supply chain strategy to conform to

questions.text: How does tracing the information, product, cash and reverse flows help a design effort?

options.text: It produces the network optimisation model directly
It replaces the need for a benefit-cost analysis of technology
It fixes the transport mode for each lane
It shows who is affected, and therefore who has to be involved in the design

questions.text: A company sells both stable functional products and fast-changing fashion lines. What is the recommended configuration?

options.text: Adopt a responsive chain throughout, since it covers both cases
Standardise on one chain to protect scale economies
Assess each market and run multiple chains matched to the strategy each one needs
Outsource the fashion line, because no single chain can serve it

questions.text: Design objectives are defined during the planning phase of the chain's core processes. Which processes does that phase set the direction for?

options.text: Forecasting, budgeting and capacity planning
Source, make, deliver, return and enable
Purchasing, manufacturing and distribution only
Sales, marketing and after-sales service

questions.text: An improvement programme proposes to measure and benchmark every process in the chain at once. What is the recommended approach instead?

options.text: Select the processes central to the strategy and focus on a small manageable number
Benchmark all processes but improve only those with external data available
Improve the processes with the lowest current cost first
Delay all measurement until the information architecture is replaced

questions.text: A technology proposal is challenged on whether it will actually deliver. Which 3 conditions have to hold at the same time?

options.text: The right budget, the right vendor and the right timetable
The right hardware, the right software and the right network
The right payback, the right risk profile and the right sponsor
The right technology applied to the right process by the right people

lessons.title: 5 - Information Architecture and Network Configuration
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: An organisation shifts from a departmental focus to an extended process focus but leaves its information system architecture unchanged. What is the likely outcome?

options.text: The older architecture prevents the change from succeeding, rather than merely slowing it
The change succeeds more slowly, at higher training cost
The architecture realigns itself as new processes generate new data
The change succeeds provided the metrics are redesigned at the same time

questions.text: At the information strategy layer, what should be done about trading partners?

options.text: Mandate a common system for every partner before design begins
Perform a gap analysis with key willing partners against the envisioned system
Defer all partner questions until the infrastructure design layer
Survey every first and second tier partner to establish an average capability

questions.text: Users routinely work around a capable new system and distrust its outputs. What should be examined first?

options.text: Insufficient change management support from executives
Selection of the wrong software package for the strategic goals
Data quality, because poor data discredits otherwise useful systems
The client and server configuration, which cannot support real-time access

questions.text: An offshore sourcing decision is being justified on labour rates alone. Which risks does that comparison hide?

options.text: Currency movements, tax policy changes and tariff reclassification
Supplier quality failures, warranty exposure and recall costs
Longer product life cycles and reduced demand uncertainty
Port, airport and road capacity, rail gauge differences and border paperwork

questions.text: Why does the second half of the rule that you get what you measure matter more than the first?

options.text: Because measurement systems are always more accurate than judgement
Because unintended behaviour is a rational response to what was left unmeasured
Because metrics should be designed after the network is built
Because people improve everything that is measured, whatever the target

questions.text: An information system architecture is a model of how an organisation operates with regard to information. Which 4 factors does it consider?

options.text: Organisational functions, coordination and communication requirements, data modelling needs, and management and control structures
Hardware, software, networks and databases
Strategy, policies, infrastructure and change plans
Cost, reliability, relevance and maintainability

questions.text: At which point in information system design are the number, size and location of facilities and the allocation of space within them evaluated?

options.text: At the organisational strategy layer, before any information decision is taken
After the databases and networks have been configured
At the information content definition layer, where physical and information design stop being separate exercises
Only in the action plan produced at the end

questions.text: A regional manager proposes an additional warehouse because it would cut delivery time in that region. What does the governing principle of network configuration require?

options.text: Approval, because reduced delivery time is the primary network objective
Refusal, because additional warehouses always raise total cost
Approval if transport cost falls, which it does as facilities are added
Weighing the decision by its effect on the whole chain, including added inventory and storage space

lessons.title: 6 - Efficiency, Responsiveness and Resilience
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: Which pair of variables determines where a chain should sit between efficiency and responsiveness?

options.text: Inventory volume and demand uncertainty
Industry sector and company size
Geographic spread and number of suppliers
Average order size and transport mode

questions.text: A business competing purely on low cost argues that it needs no responsiveness at all. What is the correct response?

options.text: It is right, because efficiency and responsiveness cannot coexist
It still needs some responsiveness to mitigate demand risk
It should maximise both, because customer focus carries no cost
It should convert to a responsive chain to protect market share

questions.text: A retailer runs 3 separate chains on 3 continents and accepts higher overhead, weaker purchasing scale and higher transport cost. Which further benefit does that structure deliver?

options.text: Lower total inventory, because each brand forecasts separately
A shorter product life cycle for each brand
The 3 networks can provide backup for one another if one is disrupted
Reduced demand uncertainty, because segments buy more predictably

questions.text: A disruption is under way now and no sensing or early-warning mechanisms were built beforehand. Which resilience lever is actually available?

options.text: Flexibility, because it costs less to run than redundancy
Alignment with partners, which can be arranged during the disruption
Efficiency, because low-cost operations absorb shocks best
Redundancy, because it costs money continuously but is available immediately

questions.text: Supply chain resilience names 3 separate capabilities. Which are they, and where are most organisations weak?

options.text: Anticipate, avoid or mitigate, and recover; most are weak at the first two
Forecast, hedge and insure; most are weak at hedging
Agile, adaptable and aligned; most are weak at adaptability
Sense, respond and report; most are weak at reporting

questions.text: A response-focused planner builds the plan around system flexibility and a capacity cushion rather than a single point forecast. What is a capacity cushion?

options.text: The difference between rated and demonstrated capacity at a work centre
Inventory held to cover demand during the replenishment lead time
The share of capacity reserved for the largest customer
Extra capacity added after capacity for expected demand has been calculated

questions.text: A product line shows stable demand, a long life cycle, infrequent introductions and limited variety. Which configuration fits, and how are orders served?

options.text: A responsive chain, using assemble-to-order and multiple warehouses
A responsive chain, holding redundant capacity through supplier contracts
An efficiency-focused chain, filling customer orders from inventory
An efficiency-focused chain, filling customer orders from a make-to-order line

questions.text: A chain has driven out cost and is the lowest-cost operator in its segment. What does that establish about competitive advantage?

options.text: It secures advantage, because cost is the only sustainable basis for it
It is necessary but not sufficient; the chain also has to be agile, adaptable and aligned with its partners
It removes the need for resilience investment, because low cost absorbs shocks
It guarantees advantage for as long as demand uncertainty stays low

lessons.title: 7 - Network Optimisation
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: A stage 2 organisation buys the technology used by stage 4 networks. What is the likely result?

options.text: It becomes expensive shelfware, because collaborative capacity comes only from experience
It reaches stage 4, provided executive support is secured
It reaches stage 3 at once and stage 4 within a year
It succeeds if the leading firm mandates use across the network

questions.text: Most companies become stuck between stages 2 and 3. What is the reason?

options.text: Licence costs for enterprise systems exceed the benefit
They will not or cannot make the leap of trust that external integration requires
Internal integration has to be completed in every business unit first
Legacy requirements planning systems cannot be replaced

questions.text: Of the 7 cross-functional teams formed to move a network up a stage, which is formed first and why?

options.text: The executive team, because it sets the pace and the strategic goals
The buying team, because purchasing aggregation delivers the earliest savings
The technology team, because system connections must exist before other teams can move past concepts
The inventory team, because inventory turnover demonstrates the benefit of collaboration

questions.text: A stage 1 firm with multiple disconnected legacy systems wants to advance. Where should it begin?

options.text: With a single enterprise-wide replacement programme covering every function
By appointing a leader experienced in external integration
By piloting joint planning and replenishment with a key customer
With a phased approach starting in procurement and logistics, each typically worth 5% to 8% in savings

questions.text: A company points to its enterprise resource planning system as evidence that it operates at a higher maturity stage. What is the correct assessment?

options.text: An enterprise system alone may not be enough; a majority of the stage's characteristics have to be present
An enterprise system places a firm at stage 3 by definition
Maturity is judged only by the number of trading partners connected
Maturity cannot be assessed until a post-implementation review is complete

questions.text: A company has completed cross-functional internal integration and aligned its key measures to its goals, but has almost no external integration. What is the recommended next move?

options.text: Replace the legacy transactional systems before any external work
Appoint a supply chain leader with external integration experience and the authority to break down barriers, starting where market performance is not at risk
Pilot vendor-managed inventory with the largest customer
Form the executive team and set network-wide strategic goals

questions.text: In a network optimisation strategy, where do change management and training sit, and what has to precede the technical infrastructure?

options.text: Last, after the infrastructure is in place, and nothing precedes the infrastructure
First, before goals are set, with the conceptual model following the infrastructure
Fourth of the 6 steps, with the conceptual model built before the technical infrastructure
Second of the 6 steps, with the technical infrastructure built before the conceptual model

questions.text: Divisions within one chain sit at different maturity levels and the weakest is holding the whole network back. What do most companies do about it?

options.text: Hold every division at the level of the weakest until all can advance together
Advance the weakest division first, since it is the bottleneck
Advance every division at once to avoid internal inconsistency
Move 1 or 2 business units up first, and move the rest only if that succeeds

lessons.title: 8 - Collaborative Design and Design for Logistics
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

quiz.title: Collaborative Design and Design for Logistics

questions.text: Design activity accounts for 5% to 15% of product cost, yet about 70% of delivery cost is decided by design choices. What is the strongest conclusion?

options.text: Supply chain has to be represented in design, where most future delivery cost is committed
Design budgets should be cut, since design consumes little of product cost
Delivery cost should be managed after launch, where the 70% is actually spent
Engineering should own logistics, since its decisions determine delivery cost

questions.text: The most serious damage done by an over-the-wall design process is not the delay caused by rework. What is it?

options.text: Purchasing loses leverage because parts are specified before sourcing
Problems are built in unknowingly, and their cost is never seen because there is no alternative design to compare against
Engineering loses authority over the specification after several revision rounds
Marketing information degrades each time it passes between functions

questions.text: A key supplier offers to take the lead on the design of a branded product in exchange for a lower unit price. What is the right decision?

options.text: Accept, because greater supplier involvement improves cost and quality on average
Accept, provided a formal agreement assigns roles and responsibilities
Decline the lead role: the organisation whose brand is at stake keeps responsibility for the overall design
Decline all supplier involvement and revert to informal contribution only

questions.text: Why does collaborative design need a formal process rather than a better explanation of its benefits?

options.text: Because confidentiality agreements make informal contribution unlawful
Because informal collaboration produces no measurable cost or quality improvement
Because engineers lack the training to assess supply chain cost
Because designers and commercial managers are measured on targets that ignore supply chain cost savings

questions.text: A packaging proposal maximises the number of cases carried on each pallet. Which limits apply to that approach?

options.text: Retailers may not want larger quantities of slow movers, and density has to balance cubing out against weighing out
Master cartons must never be designed for manual handling without mechanical assistance
Standard box sizes remove the need to consider the product's own requirements
Unitisation applies only to goods shipped directly to end consumers

questions.text: In a traditional over-the-wall sequence, at what point does logistics first see the design?

options.text: With marketing, when customer needs are gathered
With purchasing, when materials are sourced
With production, when process modifications are assessed
Last, after every decision that fixes packaging and shipping cost has been taken

questions.text: Design for logistics minimises supply chain cost in 3 ways. Which set is correct?

options.text: Reduce part count, loosen tolerances and reduce handling
Minimise transport and storage cost, minimise manufacture and assembly time, and maximise standardisation
Minimise packaging cost, minimise returns and maximise pallet density
Minimise lead time, minimise inventory and maximise level of service

questions.text: A collaborative design programme has proved the concept on small projects and standardised its terms and training. Which step comes next, and why is it the one most often skipped?

options.text: Prioritise opportunities by best value, because ranking projects is politically difficult
Return to proof of concept on a larger project, because the early wins were too small to convince anyone
Formalise the processes with cross-functional teams and assigned time, because committing a share of someone's time is a real cost their manager has to agree
Publish the case studies more widely, because awareness is the binding constraint

lessons.title: 9 - Standardisation and Simplification
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: Annual demand across all variants is 18,000 units. Consolidating 9 variants to 4 moves the unit price from USD 42 to USD 36. What is the annual purchase saving?
Safety stock across 9 part numbers totals 2,700 units. Consolidating to 4 part numbers and applying the square root law, what is the resulting safety stock?

options.text: 900 units
1,200 units
1,800 units
2,025 units

questions.text: A commonality proposal shows a total annual benefit of USD 127,128 against up-front costs of USD 145,000 of engineering and USD 25,000 of stock write-off. What is the payback period?

options.text: 1.14 years
1.34 years
1.87 years
2.20 years

questions.text: If the supplier declines the volume tier, the annual benefit of that proposal falls from USD 127,128 to USD 19,128 while the up-front cost stays at USD 170,000. What is the payback then?

options.text: About 1.5 years
About 4 years
About 6 years
About 9 years

questions.text: In that proposal the purchase saving of USD 108,000 is 85% of the total annual benefit. Which single condition has to be confirmed in writing before engineering money is committed?

options.text: That engineering and requalification can be delivered for USD 145,000
That the supplier will grant the volume tier price at the consolidated quantity
That the write-off of discontinued variants will not exceed USD 25,000
That the square root law is valid for consolidating part numbers

questions.text: A power supply is designed to accept either a 110 or a 220 volt input, with only the end cable differing, so the same unit sells in every region. Which strategy is that?

options.text: Component commonality
Modularisation
Universality
Integral design

questions.text: A premium tool is designed so that every component works only in that one product, which raises unit cost but improves fit and finish. What is the correct assessment?

options.text: It is a design error, because modularity lowers cost in every case
It is modular design, because the components are purpose-built
It is acceptable only where the product has no service requirement
It is integral design, a legitimate choice that trades higher cost for style, quality and user experience

questions.text: Which change belongs to design for manufacture and assembly rather than to design for service?

options.text: Reducing the number of parts and the number of times parts have to be handled
Making frequently replaced parts accessible without training
Ensuring replacement parts are readily available through the chain
Designing an affordable warranty programme

lessons.title: 10 - Quality, Customisation, Sustainability and the Life Cycle
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

quiz.title: Quality, Customisation, Sustainability and the Life Cycle

questions.text: Engineering says the unit conforms to requirements, sales says it is not fit for use, and the commercial team says it is not excellent at an acceptable price. How is that argument resolved?

options.text: All 3 are valid definitions of quality, and naming which one each side is using ends the argument
Only conformance to requirements is defensible in a design review
Defect data settles it, which favours the engineering position
Quality of design and quality of conformance cannot both apply to one product

questions.text: A specification demands a tool that is both lighter and sturdier. What does quality function deployment contribute to that conflict?

options.text: It resolves it by defaulting to the conformance definition of quality
It shows the interactions between desired characteristics so conflicts can be prioritised
It sets a defect target of 3.4 per million opportunities for both attributes
It removes the conflict by deferring the choice to the production schedule

questions.text: A product line has only 2 end variants and stable demand. What is the likely effect of applying postponement?

options.text: Pipeline inventory falls proportionally, whatever the level of variety
It is the strongest available answer to residual forecast error
It can raise costs, because postponement pays for variety and here there is very little
It is a prerequisite for any form of mass customisation

questions.text: About 70% of the cost of building something new is materials and 30% is labour. Why does that make remanufacture attractive?

options.text: It removes the labour component by automating disassembly
It allows the item to be marketed as new at full price
It converts warranty expense into a source of revenue
It attacks the larger cost component by reclaiming products after one or more life cycles

questions.text: Sales are falling as the market saturates and unit costs are rising. Which change suits an organisation currently running make-to-stock?

options.text: Increase promotional spending to defend share, as in the growth stage
Hold make-to-stock, because brand loyalty will sustain volume
Transition to make-to-order to prolong profitability as long as possible
Move to engineer-to-order to capture the remaining premium customers

questions.text: A manufacturer stops shipping regionally finished units and instead ships modular parts to regional distributors for final assembly. What does that require of those distributors?

options.text: Equipment and expertise to assemble, where previously they only warehoused and distributed
Additional warehouse space only, since assembly is unchanged
A separate forecast for every finished configuration
A longer order lead time quoted to every customer

questions.text: A design team lists its provisions for end of life. Which ranking is correct on environmental impact?

options.text: Recycling first, because processing recovers more material than reuse
Reuse before recycling, because it involves less processing or none at all
Design for landfill where materials are cheap, since transport is avoided
Reuse and recycling are equivalent, so cost should decide

questions.text: A business assumes the specification developed for its most demanding market is right everywhere. Which findings contradict that assumption?

options.text: Developing markets evolve exactly as wealthy ones did, and their products stay local
Developing markets reject breakthrough innovation, and low-price products damage the brand
Developing markets need higher specifications, and premium products transfer downward easily
Developing markets adopt breakthrough innovation with less money to spend, and products built for them open new markets in developed countries

lessons.title: 11 - Technology Design
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.
