questions.text: The IT department offers to prepare the justification for a new supply chain system. What is the correct arrangement?

options.text: The recipient of the technology owns the business case, using IT staff as expert resources
IT should own it, since only IT can size the technical cost
Finance should own it, because the calculation is a discounted cash flow
The vendor should prepare it, since it holds the benchmark data

questions.text: A team is choosing between a purchased licence and a subscription service for a system that needs heavy specialisation and complex real-time integration. What follows?

options.text: The subscription service, because it removes installation and upgrade effort
A purchased package, because gaps in customisation and integration make the subscription model less suitable here
Either, since the two models differ only in how payment is scheduled
The subscription service, because access ending with payment limits the downside

questions.text: A proposal claims savings from reducing headcount once the system is live. How should that benefit be handled?

options.text: Accepted as a tangible direct saving, since salaries are easy to quantify
Excluded entirely, because employee costs are sunk
Treated with caution and positioned as workforce redeployment
Recorded as an intangible benefit, where quantification is not required

questions.text: A manager argues that assigning salaried staff to a project costs nothing, because their salaries are already committed. What is the correct response?

options.text: Correct, because sunk costs are excluded from marginal analysis
Correct, provided the staff stay within their existing reporting line
Wrong: internal staff should never be used where a consultant is available
Wrong: the salary is sunk but the time is not, because that time has an alternative use

questions.text: A 5-year case shows total benefits of USD 1,200,000, of which USD 195,000 is intangible, against total costs of USD 900,000. What is the benefit-cost ratio on tangible benefits only?
A 5-year case shows total benefits of USD 1,200,000 against total costs of USD 900,000. What is the return on the money invested, and what is it once annualised?

options.text: 33.3% in each of the 5 years
133% over the 5 years, about 18.5% a year
33.3% over the 5 years, about 5.9% a year once annualised
25% over the 5 years, about 4.6% a year once annualised

questions.text: A 5-year proposal shows benefits of USD 1,500,000, including USD 300,000 of intangibles, against costs of USD 1,000,000. Recomputed on tangible benefits only, what is the return over the period?
When should a post-implementation review be agreed, and what does agreeing it then change?

options.text: In the initial project plan, because agreeing at the outset that the outcome will be measured changes behaviour during the project
After go-live, so that the review is not influenced by project optimism
Only if the benefit-cost ratio falls below 1.00 after launch
At the vendor's discretion, since the vendor holds the performance data

lessons.title: 12 - Wrap-up
lessons.body: A recap of the release, and what it sets you up to do next.

modules.title: Systems, Communication and Projects
modules.audience: ERP and systems project leads, digital and data owners, project managers running supply chain change

lessons.title: 0 - Introduction
lessons.body: What this release covers, and who it is for.

lessons.title: 1 - ERP Systems
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: A supply chain with no agreed priorities is about to install an enterprise resources planning system in the hope that it will impose order. What is wrong with that expectation?

options.text: Planning functions cannot be switched on before the financial ledgers are live
Without vision or direction the system is only a set of applications; it amplifies the direction that already exists
The system will impose the vendor's own strategy, which rarely suits an oilfield business
Visibility only becomes available once every partner in the chain is connected

questions.text: Planning, purchasing, logistics and sales all work from one location record. What makes that possible?

options.text: Nightly batch jobs synchronise the copy held by each application
Each function holds its own master copy and differences are reconciled at period end
A shared central database lets every application create, access and modify the same data
Interface software translates each function's version of the record into a common format

questions.text: A manager argues that sharing one material master across purchasing, planning and logistics carries a risk as well as a benefit. What is the risk?

options.text: An error in the record is wrong for every function at the same moment and in the same way
Each function needs a different unit of measure, so one record cannot serve them all
Access has to be granted so widely that transaction security cannot be maintained
Purchasing will overwrite planning data whenever the two disagree

questions.text: A firm wants to shift from a product-oriented push model to a customer-oriented pull model. Its planning system was built for push. What does the change require?

options.text: A configuration change, since push and pull are parameter settings
Customisation of the current release to add pull logic to planning
A best-of-breed planning application bolted onto the existing system
A version upgrade, because best practices are built into the system's conceptual model

questions.text: Which capability makes sure that product design changes follow an authorisation procedure before they take effect?

options.text: Engineering change control
Supplier relationship management
Advanced planning and scheduling
Master production scheduling

questions.text: A warehousing application is available both from the incumbent system vendor and from a specialist. What is the strongest argument for buying from the specialist?

options.text: It will be covered by the existing support contract
It will need less user training than the incumbent's version
It will carry a lower total cost of ownership in most cases
The specialist may have far more expertise in warehousing than a generalist vendor

questions.text: Which activity counts as configuration rather than customisation?

options.text: Reprogramming an application so it reproduces a legacy approval workflow
Populating entry fields and lists with the firm's cost centres and customer codes
Adding code so the software performs a task it was never designed to do
Rewriting a standard report because the vendor's layout is unfamiliar to users

questions.text: Two packages are shortlisted. One meets 84% of the stated requirements, the other 62%. Why does the second carry a much larger cost risk?

options.text: A lower fit forces the firm to buy more user licences to cover the gaps
Support contracts are priced against the proportion of functionality used
Vendors design to cover roughly the top 80% of requested functionality, and cost rises quickly below that because of the customisation needed
Configuration effort rises in direct proportion to the number of unmet requirements

lessons.title: 2 - Advanced Planning and Scheduling
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: Several workshops in different countries can perform the same redress and the client does not care which one does it. Which question can an advanced planning and scheduling system answer that a transactional system cannot?

options.text: What each site currently holds, has committed and has on order
Which site should do the work, and when
What the redress should be priced at for the client
Whether each workshop's transactions have posted correctly

questions.text: An advanced planning system has derived an optimised production plan for a network of sites. What happens next?

options.text: It records the resulting inventory transactions itself
It instructs the suppliers directly and confirms the orders
The plan is held until the next strategic planning cycle
It passes the plan and the optimal start dates back to the transactional systems, which work out the detail

questions.text: Deciding where to place factories, warehouses and distribution centres, and which links to contract out, is planning at which level?

options.text: Strategic
Tactical
Operational
Transactional

questions.text: Beyond producing a workable plan, what does the requirements optimisation function add?

options.text: It executes the chosen plan across sites without planner review
It holds the costs and physical characteristics of products and resources
It generates several planning options and evaluates them against each other
It forecasts demand from order history, seasonality and marketing events

questions.text: A customer wants more than the uncommitted stock, but the balance could be manufactured in time at another site. Which promise answers that request?

options.text: Capable-to-promise, which commits orders against capacity as well as inventory
Available-to-promise, the uncommitted part of inventory and planned production
Profitable-to-promise, which adds a profitability analysis
Resource allocation, which releases the optimised requirements

questions.text: A large order can be delivered on time, but the terms demanded look thin once freight, expediting and handling are counted. Which capability answers whether to take it?

options.text: Available-to-promise
Capable-to-promise
Demand management
Profitable-to-promise

questions.text: A firm runs long-range aggregate planning in one system and short-term detailed scheduling in another, on different cycles. Which benefit of an advanced planning system addresses that directly?

options.text: It removes the need for a master production schedule at each site
It builds holistic plans that carry long-range aggregate planning and short-term scheduling together
It reduces the number of suppliers that have to be managed
It replaces the transactional system's inventory records with optimised balances

questions.text: A firm with a suspect material master wants to buy an optimiser. What sequence should it follow, and why?

options.text: Buy the optimiser first, because it will expose the data errors quickly
Build the interfaces first, because integration matters more than data quality
Correct the data first, then connect the systems, because the benefits depend on complete and accurate input
Run the optimiser beside manual planning indefinitely so every result is checked

lessons.title: 3 - Supply Chain Event Management
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: What does event management change about a manager's working day?

options.text: A faster daily report arrives covering every event in the chain
Each transaction is approved by the manager before it is posted
Business rules are set once and the manager then works exceptions instead of sifting events
Performance measurement is replaced by continuous monitoring

questions.text: Fill rate has fallen for 3 consecutive months. What does event management give a manager that a dashboard does not?

options.text: The events that caused the fall, fed into performance management so root causes can be corrected
The trend in fill rate presented in real time rather than monthly
A longer history of fill rate for periodic management review
The same fill rate figure presented to every channel and partner

questions.text: An exception flags a component shortage and the system offers to ship from an alternate source before the schedule is affected. Which of the five active visibility functions is that?

options.text: Monitor
Measure
Simulate
Control

questions.text: A shortage alert is generated correctly but reaches the planner after the replenishment decision has already been taken. What is the practical status of that alert?

options.text: An exception report, since the shortage was detected accurately
A record rather than an alert, because notification has to arrive in time to change the plan
A measure, because it can still be counted against the service target
A control, because the system can reverse the decision afterwards

questions.text: Which saving from event management is easiest to defend in a business case?

options.text: Lower customer service cost, because status information reaches customers and internal staff without a telephone call
Lower purchase prices, because suppliers compete for exception volume
Lower warehouse rent, because stock is held at fewer locations
Lower software maintenance, because the planning system is used less

questions.text: Why is redirecting a supplier shipment at the port of entry treated as such a large saving?

options.text: Customs clearance is cheaper at a port than at a distribution centre
The decision is taken while the goods are still moving, avoiding a trip to a central point and back out again
Port handling is performed by the carrier at no cost to the shipper
Sorting imported goods at a central distribution centre is not permitted

questions.text: A surgeon authorises a procedure and the system allocates nursing time, theatre and recovery space, pharmacy items and meals. What capability does that illustrate?

options.text: Exception reporting against business rules
Measurement of events against performance indicators
One event triggering downstream activity rather than only reporting it
Dynamic updating of distributed databases across partners

questions.text: A firm at an early stage of supply chain development wants to buy event management to leapfrog its competitors. What is the sound response?

options.text: It is the fastest available route from an early stage to an integrated chain
It works at any stage, because it needs only exception rules and alerts
It should be deferred until the chain has already reached the highest stage
It helps a chain reach the highest stage, so it suits a firm whose functional systems are already integrated

lessons.title: 4 - Warehouse Management Systems
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: Warehouse system functionality now overlaps light manufacturing, transportation, labour and order management. What should a selection decision hinge on?

options.text: The vendor offering the widest functional coverage across those areas
The application offered by the incumbent enterprise system vendor
The strength of the labour and order management functionality
Directed picking, directed replenishment and directed put-away

questions.text: A warehouse system, a new layout and hand-held scanning are all being introduced. What has to be settled before the work starts?

options.text: A joint map of the system, the layout and every enabling device, including where scanners will be mounted
The training plan for pickers, which sets the pace of the rollout
The choice between radio frequency identification and bar codes for all items
The service level agreement with the software vendor

questions.text: Which inventory counting capability should be insisted on when a warehouse system is specified?

options.text: An annual physical count reconciled to the ledger
Continuous cycle counting
Quarterly counts of the highest-value items only
A count triggered whenever a picker reports a discrepancy

questions.text: A warehouse system directs work from item, quantity, location, unit of measure and order data. Which of those is most often unreliable, and what follows?

options.text: Location, so put-away instructions become approximate
Quantity, so cycle counts never reconcile
Unit of measure, so every instruction the system issues is suspect
Order data, so pick plans are sequenced incorrectly

questions.text: Slow-moving surplus occupies rack space worth more than the picking travel it would save. Which storage logic fits?

options.text: Pick-to-clear, which uses the smallest quantities first to free space
Nearest location, to minimise travel for pickers
Fewest locations, so nobody has to search for the item
Zone logic, confining the item to one defined storage zone

questions.text: Which warehouse function tracks items by batch or lot, places rejects on hold and notifies management of issues?

options.text: Inventory control
Receiving
Quality control
Storage location management and optimisation

questions.text: Two firms operating in the same region each carry unused rack space and unused outbound capacity. Which capability lets them use it?

options.text: Pick-to-light and voice direction inside each site
Web portals that support merge-in-transit and cross-company sharing of space and freight
Continuous cycle counting across both inventories
Directed put-away tuned to each firm's velocity profile

questions.text: Why does a warehouse system business case often look marginal at approval?

options.text: Hardware and software costs are systematically overstated by vendors
The benefits accrue to customers rather than to the warehouse
Cycle time gains cannot be measured until well after go-live
The costs it removes, such as wrong picks, rush orders and deliberate over-picking, appear in no line item

lessons.title: 5 - Transportation Management Systems
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: Which change in order patterns made transportation management systems integral to supply chain management?

options.text: Smaller and more frequent orders, driven by online buying, just-in-time and build-to-order
Larger consolidated orders placed against annual contracts
A general shift from road movement to intermodal movement
The replacement of common carriers by private fleets

questions.text: A transportation system produces well optimised routes and operations quietly ignores them. Which of the five things such a package must provide is missing?

options.text: Visibility for managers, sales staff, customers and shipping personnel
Integration between transportation planning and order fulfilment
Execution control, which confirms the plan is actually being followed
Automation, which raises efficiency and reduces errors

questions.text: Freight is currently tendered lane by lane in a spreadsheet, each lane at its lowest quote. What does centralised shipment planning add?

options.text: A single carrier for all lanes, which simplifies administration
Holistic optimisation of routes, modes, freight cost, lead time and service together
Automatic payment of freight bills without audit
A fixed routing guide reviewed once a year by procurement

questions.text: A firm works with a very large number of transportation suppliers. Which strategy follows from that?

options.text: Tender every load on an open marketplace to guarantee the lowest price
Consolidate all volume with a single carrier to maximise leverage
Award lanes by rotation so no carrier becomes indispensable
Key partnerships with a small number of suppliers for most activity, and marketplaces for the exceptions

questions.text: In the freight rating function, on what basis does the system choose between carriers?

options.text: The lowest rate tariff quoted for the lane
Service level ratings updated from past cost, on-time delivery, and errors or damage
The carrier's position in a routing guide set annually by procurement
The demurrage and per diem rates agreed in the carrier contract

questions.text: Which transportation system function most reliably pays for the system, and why is it so often left unused?

options.text: Freight bill audit, because nobody finds the time to configure it
Manifesting, because label printers are rarely integrated
Network design, because it is only run when strategy changes
Load tendering, because carriers resist an ordered preference list

questions.text: A consignment is in transit when the receiving site is closed by an incident and the goods are needed elsewhere. What does a web-based transportation system allow?

options.text: Nothing until the load is delivered and re-consigned as a new shipment
A claim against the carrier for the additional movement
The destination to be changed in transit, with a notice of consignment and revised charges
A manual instruction to the driver, recorded afterwards as an exception

questions.text: A request for proposal sent through a carrier network to nearly 500 carriers saved USD 3.9 million, about 4% of annual transportation spend. Roughly what was that spend?

options.text: USD 15.6 million
USD 39 million
USD 156 million
USD 97.5 million

lessons.title: 6 - Data Capture
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: Who should own the decision about which data are captured, where and how?

options.text: The warehouse or base that operates the devices, since it knows the process
Senior management, because setting the methods, policies and procedures is a strategic decision
The system vendor, because capture options depend on the hardware
The finance function, because capture cost falls in its budget

questions.text: A base can capture reliable data for only part of its inventory. What is the right course?

options.text: Start with the part that can be captured, because partial data give incremental gains and show what to capture next
Wait until complete visibility across the network can be achieved in one step
Capture everything manually until an automated solution is funded
Restrict capture to the highest-value items permanently

questions.text: A consumable is issued at a well site and the movement is written on a paper ticket that is keyed in 3 days later. What has the firm actually got?

options.text: Accurate data with an acceptable delay
A batch capture process that needs a faster keying cycle
History rather than a demand signal, because the data were not captured at the source
A control weakness that a second signature would resolve

questions.text: Why is passive or automatic capture treated as more reliable than a manual process?

options.text: It removes the need for any verification of the captured data
It captures a wider range of fields than a person would record
It can be audited, whereas manual entries cannot
It is more likely to happen every time, and manual capture fails precisely when people are busy

questions.text: Defective items must be traced to an individual serial number, and the label area available is small. Which coding choice suits?

options.text: A two-dimensional code, which stores data horizontally and vertically and can carry a serial number
A 12-digit linear code identifying manufacturer and stock keeping unit
A linear code read omnidirectionally by an optical scanner
A printed part number checked visually at receipt

questions.text: Radio frequency tags on steel components in a fluids store are being read inconsistently. What are the appropriate remedies?

options.text: Increase the number of tags on each item so at least one is read
Reposition readers and antennae, add shielding, or change the tag or reader type to suit the product
Move to a fully manual count and abandon automatic capture
Raise reader power until read rates reach an acceptable level

questions.text: A firm early in its supply chain development proposes a full radio frequency identification rollout. What is the likely outcome?

options.text: Read rates will stay low until warehouse staff are retrained
Interference from metal and liquid will make the project fail outright
It will incur all of the costs and none of the benefits, because it cannot use the information gathered
Payback will only arrive once bar codes are withdrawn entirely

questions.text: Capturing the point of sale or point of use is said to reduce the bullwhip effect. What condition is attached?

options.text: The data must be aggregated by region before release
The firm must already be operating vendor-managed inventory
The data must be captured by radio frequency identification rather than by code
The data must be shared promptly along the chain rather than held internally

lessons.title: 7 - Databases, Middleware and Communications
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: Why are hierarchical databases now little used?

options.text: Associating records in different branches requires duplicated data, and the copies diverge
They cannot hold more than one type of record within a branch
They allow a child record to have several parents, which creates ambiguity
They cannot be distributed across geographically dispersed servers

questions.text: Part number appears in an order table, a part table and a supplier table. What rule governs that?

options.text: Each table keeps its own copy and a nightly routine reconciles them
The field must be removed from all but one table to remove redundancy
The field is managed in exactly one table; the others display it without owning it
Whichever system writes the field most often is treated as its owner

questions.text: A firm mapped one partner's system field by field and now wants to connect two more partners on different systems. What is the drawback of continuing that way?

options.text: Field-level mapping cannot carry order or invoice data
Each new link starts from scratch, and the mapping has to be redone after upgrades
It requires all partners to run the same enterprise system
It prevents secure authentication between the linked systems

questions.text: 8 partners on 8 different systems need to exchange the same order and shipment information. Which approach suits, and why?

options.text: Custom-programmed links, because they can be tuned to each partner
Field-by-field data mapping, because it gives fast communication between each pair
Replacing the partners' systems so no translation is needed
Process-oriented middleware, because each system maps once to a standard process

questions.text: Which side benefit of process-oriented middleware is often worth as much as the integration itself?

options.text: It forces the businesses to articulate and simplify their processes
It removes the need for authentication and authorisation controls
It eliminates the need to agree message formats with partners
It replaces the enterprise system's transaction records

questions.text: How is electronic data interchange best characterised?

options.text: A process-oriented approach that manages whole conversations between systems
A content-level method in which parties agree a shared format for standard documents and fields
A framework that moves data without any direct connection between applications
A set of reusable services assembled into applications

questions.text: Why are web-services-based offerings displacing electronic data interchange for the more demanding supply chain messages?

options.text: Standard document formats have been withdrawn from use
Advanced shipment notifications can no longer be carried
Regulators now require web protocols for cross-border trade
The older method is expensive to implement, often batch-driven, and too costly for complex messaging such as event management

questions.text: A service-oriented design requires every message to carry all the data needed to complete processing. Which goal does that serve?

options.text: Loose coupling, so services can be assembled and separated easily
Backward compatibility with existing document formats
Universal functionality, achieved by separating applications from their data
Tighter binding between an application and its host platform

lessons.title: 8 - Data Accuracy and Analysis
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: Cube and weight data are wrong for a small proportion of items, and the transportation system begins recommending overloaded vehicles. What is the most serious cost?

options.text: The freight paid on the loads that were built incorrectly
The time spent tracing and correcting the affected records
The penalties for exceeding vehicle weight limits
Loss of trust in a system that has already been paid for, and its eventual abandonment

questions.text: A planner receives accurate consumption data 4 days after the replenishment decision was due. How should that be treated?

options.text: As wrong data, because late information produces the same decision as inaccurate information
As accurate data with a reporting lag that can be corrected in the next cycle
As a formatting problem to be raised with the sending system
As acceptable, provided the figures reconcile at month end

questions.text: Two item databases are being merged and the duplicated structures are producing logical anomalies. Which remedy addresses that?

options.text: Data cleansing, which finds and fixes misspellings, gaps and false values
Data normalisation, which minimises duplication and guards against structural anomalies
Aggregation, which groups records into like categories
Role-based limits on adding, deleting and modifying records

questions.text: When should data cleansing and normalisation be scheduled relative to a system upgrade?

options.text: Well before it, so the upgrade starts from a clean base
Afterwards, once the new system shows which data actually matter
Combined with it, as one initiative
Only if the upgrade fails to deliver the expected return

questions.text: A supplier of raw sand is given its customer's demand expressed in sheets of finished abrasive paper. What is wrong with that?

options.text: The data are commercially sensitive and should not be shared at all
Finished goods demand is less accurate than component demand
The customer should aggregate the data before sharing it
Shared data must be presented in terms relevant to the receiver, so it should be in kilograms of sand

questions.text: Sales by item by site shows large and confusing variation. What does aggregating to regional level achieve, and why?

options.text: It reduces relative variance by pooling random variables, so trends and averages become clearer
It removes the errors introduced each time the data were manipulated
It increases the detail available for operational decisions
It removes the need to validate the model against historical results

questions.text: A dispatcher needs a re-planning answer within minutes, several times a shift. What sort of decision support suits that need?

options.text: A detailed model using the most extensive history available
A simpler model working on current data, built for speed
The same model used for network design, run more frequently
A model that trades off qualitative objectives before answering

questions.text: A planning model run on current data returns a surprising result. Why does the historical test have to come first?

options.text: Because historical data sets are more complete than current ones
Because auditors require a documented run on historical data
Otherwise there is no way to tell whether the surprise lies in the model or in the business
Because aggregation error can only be estimated from history

lessons.title: 9 - Electronic Business
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: How do electronic business and electronic commerce relate?

options.text: They are interchangeable terms for trading over the internet
Electronic commerce is the whole; electronic business is its business-to-business part
Electronic business is the whole; electronic commerce is the transacting part of it
Electronic business covers consumer models and electronic commerce covers business models

questions.text: An online channel is expected to strengthen a firm's competitive position. What should be expected to happen to its costs?

options.text: Every cost category falls, which is why the channel pays for itself
Inventory, facility and transaction costs fall, while transportation and technology costs rise
Transportation costs fall, because inbound flows can be centralised
Costs hold level while revenue rises through wider reach

questions.text: Why does outbound transportation cost rise when a firm sells online?

options.text: Carriers charge a premium for consumer deliveries
Inbound consolidation is no longer available once orders are placed online
Returns have to be moved by a separate provider
Customers no longer collect, so the firm ships smaller quantities of a wider range, more often, to more places

questions.text: Why do materials-handling costs rise in the same move?

options.text: Actions the customer used to perform, such as picking, packaging and handling returns, now fall to the firm
Handling equipment has to be automated to cope with the volume
Warehouses must be relocated closer to airports
Returns must be inspected by an independent provider

questions.text: Several well-funded online ventures failed despite heavy national advertising. What did they have in common?

options.text: They separated the electronic business from the physical business, producing an inefficient network and an inconsistent message
They spent too little on marketing to establish their brands
They relied on membership-based exchanges rather than open ones
They entered their markets before connectivity could support them

questions.text: A campaign is expected to lift traffic through a firm's exchange sharply. Where is that volume actually paid for?

options.text: The application layer, holding catalogues, carts and billing tools
The aggregation layer, where portals and brokers package services
The foundation layer, where setup and maintenance must carry the traffic
The business layer, where the buying and selling occurs

questions.text: 6 firms in a chain each exchange data directly with the other 5. How many separate links is that, and how many if all 6 trade through a single exchange hub?

options.text: 30 links, reduced to 6
15 links, reduced to 6
15 links, reduced to 5
36 links, reduced to 12

questions.text: A firm buys safety-critical items and is considering trading through an exchange. Which distinction matters most?

options.text: Whether the exchange is hosted by a vendor or by a consortium
Whether the exchange supports document standards or web services
Whether the exchange charges sellers to list
Whether it is an open exchange, or a membership-based exchange that prescreens its members

lessons.title: 10 - Communications
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: A colleague replies that they have received your email. Which element of the communication process is that, and what does it not establish?

options.text: Acknowledgment, which signals receipt but not comprehension or agreement
Feedback, which confirms the message was understood as intended
Decoding, which shows the receiver has interpreted the message correctly
A filter, which shows the message arrived without distortion

questions.text: Feedback shows that an instruction was not understood as intended. What should the sender do?

options.text: Resend the original message through a second medium
Escalate it through the formal chain of command
Obtain written acknowledgment from every recipient
Revise the message and repeat the communication process

questions.text: Why should informal communication not be underestimated in a project?

options.text: It is officially sanctioned and therefore well documented
Most communication in an organisation is informal, so most information moves that way
It follows the official chain of command more closely than formal channels
Amendments to it are restricted once it has been issued

questions.text: A rollout has 9 stakeholders. Using channels equal to n times n minus 1, divided by 2, how many communication channels are there?
3 more sites join that rollout, taking the group from 9 stakeholders to 12. What are the two increases?

options.text: 33% more people and 83% more channels
33% more people and 33% more channels
25% more people and 55% more channels
33% more people and 183% more channels

questions.text: A group of 12 stakeholders carries 66 channels. The parties agree to nominate 6 authorised representatives. By roughly how much does the channel count fall?

options.text: About 50%
About 55%
About 88%
About 77%

questions.text: A rollout update is emailed to everyone in the firm in the hope that the people affected will notice it. What is the consequence?

options.text: Wider circulation improves the chance that the right people act
Intent is diluted, and the result is indifference and confusion
The message becomes a formal communication because of its distribution
Feedback improves, because more recipients can respond

questions.text: You will recommend cutting the number of authorised representatives on a struggling project. What must the recommendation also state?

options.text: The cost of the software licences that will be released
The date on which the reduced group will be reviewed
What is given up, namely that fewer people will feel heard
The names of the stakeholders who objected

lessons.title: 11 - Project Management: Plan and Design
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: A firm builds a second warehouse to the same design as the first, on a different plot and with different contractors. Is that a project?

options.text: No, because the design is repeated, so the work is an operation
No, because the deliverable is tangible rather than a service or result
Yes, because it is temporary and the plot and contractors make the result unique
Yes, but only if it runs longer than one financial year

questions.text: A team member argues that a necessary task can proceed even though it does not appear in the work breakdown structure. What is the correct position?

options.text: It may proceed provided it stays within the approved cost baseline
The structure maps 100% of the work, so if the task is not on it, it is not being done
The structure lists activities, so the task belongs in the schedule instead
It may proceed once the sponsor gives verbal approval

questions.text: Which sequencing error is most often made when a project schedule is built?

options.text: Estimating activity durations before the resources and their level of expertise are known
Decomposing the scope before the requirements have been agreed
Developing the budget at the same time as the schedule
Setting acceptance criteria before requirements are measurable

questions.text: A sponsor insists a project can be delivered for 20% less than the best planning estimate, with no change to scope or schedule. What is the project manager's responsibility?

options.text: Accept the figure and manage to it, since the sponsor holds the budget
Accept it and record a risk against the shortfall
Reduce the contingency until the numbers meet the target
Push back, and either secure the additional funding or decline to lead the project

questions.text: Activities: A 4 weeks (start); B 6 (after A); C 8 (after A); D 5 (after B); E 6 (after A); F 3 (after C, D, E); G 2 (after E); H 1 (after F, G). What is the shortest possible duration?

options.text: 16 weeks
19 weeks
22 weeks
35 weeks

questions.text: A network has a critical path of 19 weeks. A second path runs A 4 weeks, E 6 weeks, G 2 weeks, H 1 week. How much float does that path carry?

options.text: Zero, since A and H are also on the critical path
3 weeks
6 weeks
13 weeks

questions.text: Critical path A-B-D-F-H runs 19 weeks and go-live is wanted in 17. Crash costs per week: A USD 12,000 (max 1), B USD 9,000 (max 3), D USD 14,000 (max 2), F USD 20,000 (max 1). Cheapest option?

options.text: Crash B by 2 weeks, for USD 18,000
Crash A by 1 week and D by 1 week, for USD 26,000
Crash D by 2 weeks, for USD 28,000
Crash the 8-week data cleansing activity by 2 weeks at the lowest available rate

questions.text: Crashing B by its full 3 weeks brings A-B-D-F-H to 16 weeks, but A-C-F-H is also 16 weeks. What follows for any further reduction?

options.text: Crash B further, since it remains the cheapest activity per week
Crash C, because it is now the longest single activity in the network
No further reduction is possible by crashing
Only crashing an activity both paths share, A, F or H, will shorten the project

lessons.title: 12 - Project Management: Execute and Control
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: A rollout has a budget of USD 2,400,000 for 8 sites over 16 months, with work spread evenly. At the end of month 10, 4 sites are complete and USD 1,300,000 is spent. What is the schedule variance?

options.text: Negative USD 300,000, so behind schedule
Negative USD 100,000, so behind schedule
Positive USD 200,000, so ahead of schedule
Negative USD 200,000, so behind schedule

questions.text: On a project the earned value is USD 1,200,000, the actual cost USD 1,300,000 and the planned value USD 1,500,000. Which problem is larger, and by how much?

options.text: The cost problem, by USD 200,000
The cost problem, by USD 100,000
The schedule problem, which at USD 300,000 exceeds the USD 100,000 cost overrun
Neither, because the two variances offset each other

questions.text: Budget USD 2,400,000, earned value USD 1,200,000, actual cost USD 1,300,000. What is the estimate at completion?

options.text: USD 2,400,000, because the budget has not yet been exceeded
USD 2,600,000, an overrun of about 8%
USD 2,500,000, the budget plus the amount overspent so far
USD 2,215,000, the budget multiplied by the cost performance index

questions.text: A project was planned to take 16 months. Earned value is USD 1,200,000 against a planned value of USD 1,500,000. What is the forecast duration?

options.text: 16 months, since the schedule baseline has not been changed
18 months
17 months
20 months

questions.text: A finance report shows USD 1,300,000 spent against USD 1,500,000 planned by month 10, and concludes the project is under budget. Only 4 of the 8 sites are complete against 5 planned. What is actually happening?

options.text: The project is behind schedule and over budget; the apparent underspend reflects work not done
The project is under budget and slightly behind schedule, which the underspend offsets
The project is on budget, since the variance is within 15% of plan
The project is ahead on cost and the site count will recover in the remaining months

questions.text: Why are audits of processes preferred to inspection of deliverables as a control activity?

options.text: Inspection of deliverables is optional once quality metrics are defined
Reviewing processes while they run prevents problems, whereas inspection finds them when only rework remains
Process audits are performed by the customer rather than by the team
Deliverable inspection belongs to closure rather than to control

questions.text: What is the relationship between the number of processes in the executing group and the effort spent there?

options.text: It has more processes than planning and consumes the most time and resources
It has more processes than planning but consumes less time than planning
It has fewer processes than planning yet consumes the largest share of time and resources
It has fewer processes than planning and a correspondingly smaller share of effort

questions.text: A sponsor cancels a supply chain project at the halfway point. What now has to happen?

options.text: The remaining budget is returned and the files are archived without review
Closure is skipped, because no deliverables were handed over
Lessons learned are recorded only if the sponsor asks for them
It is formally closed: contracts closed, final payments made, people released and lessons recorded

lessons.title: 13 - Wrap-up
lessons.body: A recap of the release, and what it sets you up to do next.

modules.title: Metrics, Improvement and Change
modules.audience: Anyone who owns a KPI or a dashboard, continuous improvement and quality leads, operations managers

lessons.title: 0 - Introduction
lessons.body: What this release covers, and who it is for.

lessons.title: 1 - Why Measure At All
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: An organisation gathers accurate performance data every month and publishes it, but never compares it against standards and never acts on it. What does it actually have?

options.text: A reporting function rather than a measurement system
A control system missing only its directing objective
A complete measurement system operating at a minimum acceptable level
A directing system that lacks monitoring

questions.text: The directing objective requires an understanding of actual human motivation rather than assumed motivation. Why does that distinction matter?

options.text: Because directing exists to report fairly on individual performance
Because measurement changes behaviour, so a misread incentive produces consequences nobody chose
Because motivation research has to be finished before any data is gathered
Because performance standards cannot be set without surveying the workforce

questions.text: A proposed metric would drive exactly the behaviour NESR wants, but collecting the data would cost more than the behaviour is worth. What follows?

options.text: Adopt it, because behavioural effects always outweigh collection cost
Adopt it, because a cheap metric is always worse than an expensive one
Reject it, because feasibility and cost-effectiveness are constraints the metric also has to satisfy
Adopt it, provided the data is held in a role-restricted repository

questions.text: Which of these is a genuine supply chain metric rather than a functional measure carrying a supply chain label?

options.text: Inventory holding cost at a single warehouse
Cost containment on a single leg of a cross-country shipment
Output increase at a single plant
The speed at which information flows from the end customer back through the chain

questions.text: In analysing performance, which step comes first?

options.text: Formulating the questions the performance information has to be able to answer
Placing data in context against baselines, goals or benchmarks
Validating the analytical tools as well as the data
Choosing formats and media suited to the audience

questions.text: Comparing performance against standards serves two different purposes. Which pair is correct, and which of the two is worth more?

options.text: Reporting and archiving, with archiving the more valuable
Getting back on course and improving the course, with improving the course the more valuable
Identifying causes and assigning accountability, with accountability the more valuable
Monitoring and directing, with directing the more valuable

questions.text: Actual freight rates cannot be obtained for a lane NESR needs to measure. What is the correct response?

options.text: Drop the metric until the exact data can be purchased
Estimate the figure and record it as an actual
Use an acceptable proxy such as a distance-based rate, unless actual rates would materially change the decision
Substitute a functional measure that uses data already held

questions.text: Improving performance includes periodic audits of processes against strategic objectives. What else is explicitly audited?

options.text: The access permissions on the data repository
The competence of the analysts who prepared the reports
The external agencies supplying comparative data
The measurement process itself

lessons.title: 2 - Selecting Metrics That Do Not Backfire
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

quiz.title: Selecting Metrics That Do Not Backfire

questions.text: You get what you measure. Which half of that principle is close to a certainty?

options.text: That a measured goal will be achieved
That an ignored goal will not be achieved
That measuring a goal removes the need for a target value
That an unmeasured goal will be achieved by other means

questions.text: If omitting a metric costs more than including one, why is measuring everything still the wrong answer?

options.text: Because unmeasured goals get achieved informally anyway
Because each additional metric weakens the incentive carried by the others
Because it is not feasible, so managers have to choose a limited set tied to strategy
Because attributes such as velocity and visibility cannot be quantified

questions.text: A buyer measured on purchase price variance buys in bulk from the lowest bidder. Inventory rises and quality falls. Who is responsible for those two outcomes?

options.text: Whoever chose the metric
The buyer, for chasing discounts at the expense of quality
The suppliers, for bidding on terms they could not sustain
Finance, for not reporting carrying cost alongside price

questions.text: Organisations moved from purchase price variance towards value delivered to the final customer, accepting a measure that is harder and dearer to collect. What is the lesson?

options.text: Prefer cheaper measures wherever partner data is scarce
Purchase price variance has no legitimate use anywhere
Measures that need partner data are rarely worth the effort
A cheap metric that produces the wrong behaviour is not cheap

questions.text: A manager presents a metric set in which no measure pulls against any other. What does the manager actually have?

options.text: A direction, which somebody will eventually follow too far
A focused set, since conflicting measures only confuse staff
A diagnostic set, suitable for choosing between alternatives
A balanced set, provided each measure aligns with strategy

questions.text: A service line is measured only on purchase price and on-time delivery. Which addition would create the tension the set is missing?

options.text: Supplier lead time variability
Order entry accuracy
Inventory turnover and cash-to-cash cycle time
Number of active suppliers

questions.text: A published framework prioritises metrics along three continuums. What does its method assess first?

options.text: Whether each measure is diagnostic or used for monitoring
Where the organisation sits between responsive and efficient
Whether each measure is strategic or operational
Whether the measure can be shared beyond the organisation's own walls

questions.text: A new metric set is issued to suppliers and internal teams with definitions and reporting dates, but no explanation of why. What is the predictable result?

options.text: The measures will be reported late but accurately
The measures will be renegotiated at executive level
Compliance will be high, because the instructions are precise
The measures will be gamed, because a metric arriving without a reason invites it

lessons.title: 3 - Customer Metrics and the Perfect Order
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

quiz.title: Customer Metrics and the Perfect Order

questions.text: A shipment reaches the customer's gate on the promised day, but the equipment has to be installed before it can be used. Under speed of performance, when does the clock stop?

options.text: At the gate, because delivery is complete
When the invoice is settled
When the product is delivered and ready for use
When the order acknowledgement is issued

questions.text: Customer-focused measures group under availability, time to deliver, product support and overall satisfaction. Which group measures the outcome rather than what is hoped to produce it?

options.text: Availability
Time needed to deliver a customer order
Product support
Overall satisfaction

questions.text: An order arrives at the right place on the customer's requested date, complete and undamaged, but the invoice is wrong. How does the perfect order measure treat it?

options.text: Not perfect, because accurate documentation is a required condition
Perfect, because the physical delivery met every requirement
Perfect, because invoicing sits outside order fulfilment
Partly perfect, weighted by the number of conditions met

questions.text: Why is response accuracy a better product support measure than response time on its own?

options.text: Accuracy is cheaper to measure than elapsed time
A fast wrong answer simply produces a second enquiry
Response time is not a customer-focused measure
Accuracy is one of the conditions of a perfect order

questions.text: Every internal customer measure for a service line is identical to last year, yet satisfaction has fallen. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Fill rate has been calculated on the wrong denominator
The perfect order rate is being reported from a single gate
Competitors improved, so customer expectations rose
Real-time reporting has exposed problems that monthly reports concealed

questions.text: A customer requests 250 units and 215 are shipped from available stock. What is the fill rate, and what does that measure capture?

options.text: 86%, the frequency of stockouts
14%, the shortfall the customer experienced
94%, the proportion of orders shipped complete
86%, the impact of stockouts over time

questions.text: Whose date decides whether an order counts as on time in a perfect order calculation?

options.text: The customer's requested date
The date NESR acknowledged when the order was accepted
The date the carrier confirmed at collection
The promised date, adjusted for any agreed changes

questions.text: A service line ships 40,000 orders a month at 99% on time, and the executive team is content. Which report is most likely to sustain attention?

options.text: 99% on time, with a rolling 12-month average alongside
400 customers received a late order last month
4,000 customers received a late order last month
99% on time, broken down by product family

lessons.title: 4 - Financial and Cost Metrics
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: Compare adding USD 1,000,000 of sales at a 35% gross margin with removing USD 1,000,000 of supply chain cost. What reaches net profit in each case?

options.text: USD 350,000 from the sales and USD 1,000,000 from the cost removal
USD 1,000,000 from the sales and USD 350,000 from the cost removal
USD 350,000 from each, because both run through the same margin
USD 650,000 from the sales and USD 1,000,000 from the cost removal

questions.text: A team removes USD 900,000 of supply chain cost. At a 30% gross margin, how much additional revenue would be needed to deliver the same profit?
Order processing cost rose from USD 500,000 to USD 600,000 while orders handled rose from 10,000 to 15,000. What does adding volume to the cost measure show?

options.text: Cost per order rose from USD 33 to USD 40, so the activity became less efficient
Cost per order fell from USD 50 to USD 40, so the increase is volume rather than inefficiency
Cost per order was unchanged, so the whole increase is volume
Cost per order cannot be derived without a variance threshold

questions.text: When is shifting cost onto another chain participant a legitimate move?

options.text: When the shift is agreed in the contract
When your own cost as a share of net sales improves
When the receiving participant is able to finance it
When total cost across the whole chain is lower afterwards

questions.text: Procurement moves USD 500,000 of cost onto a supplier whose cost of capital is higher than NESR's. What will NESR's own measures show while that plays out?

options.text: Improvement, which is what makes this pattern hard to detect
An unfavourable purchase price variance
A rise in supply chain cost as a share of net sales
No change, because the cost was moved rather than removed

questions.text: Why do organisations set a threshold on cost variances?

options.text: Because variances below it are not genuine costs
So that only variances worth discussing trigger exception handling
Because favourable variances need no investigation
To turn a cost level into a trend that can be projected

questions.text: Chain partners will not disclose cost data because they treat it as confidential. What arrangement produces chain-level cost measurement anyway?

options.text: Benchmark against published industry averages instead
Make disclosure a condition of every contract
Have an intermediary collect the data and report only the aggregate
Measure on-shelf availability, which needs no partner data

questions.text: Fill rates for a retail chain are consistently high, yet shoppers report empty shelves. Which measure closes that gap?

options.text: Dwell time across the chain
Inventory days of supply
Order-to-receipt response time
On-shelf in-stock percentage

lessons.title: 5 - Supplier Health and Return on Assets
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

quiz.title: Supplier Health and Return on Assets

questions.text: Most leverage ratios are better when lower from a supplier solvency point of view. Which is the exception, and in which direction?

options.text: Interest coverage, which should be higher
Current debt to equity, which should be higher
The quick ratio, which should be lower
Inventory days outstanding, which should be higher

questions.text: A supplier reports sales of 120 against average inventory of 40, giving inventory turnover of 3.0. What are its inventory days outstanding, and which way should that figure move?

options.text: 3 days, and it should be rising
122 days, and it should be rising
122 days, and it should be falling
40 days, and it should be falling

questions.text: The quick ratio deducts inventories from current assets before dividing by current liabilities. Why?

options.text: Because inventory is valued inconsistently between organisations
Because the question being asked is how fast the supplier can pay, and inventory is not fast
Because inventory already appears in the activity ratios
Because inventory is financed by long-term rather than current debt

questions.text: A critical supplier is privately owned and does not publish accounts. What does that mean for the ratio analysis you planned?

options.text: Apply the public thresholds instead, since they are more conservative
Estimate the ratios from purchase order history
The analysis is unaffected, since ratios can be derived from invoices
It cannot be done unless they share the figures voluntarily, so fall back to credit reports, bank references and third-party ratings

questions.text: A privately owned supplier you cannot easily replace returns a bankruptcy risk score of 2.0. Which band is that, and what are the two available responses?

options.text: Red, so do not select it, or make it a candidate for replacement
Green, so treat it as stable and keep tracking quarterly
Yellow, so watch it closely, or give it assistance
Yellow, but the private thresholds cannot be applied to an unlisted supplier

questions.text: A service line has net sales of USD 24,000,000, net profit of USD 1,440,000 and total assets of USD 16,000,000. What is return on assets, and how does it decompose?

options.text: 6%, which is the net profit margin on its own
1.5%, which is the asset turnover on its own
7.5%, being the margin added to the turnover
9%, being a 6% margin multiplied by an asset turnover of 1.5

questions.text: Inventory falls by USD 1,200,000 at a 25% carrying rate, so total assets fall to USD 14,800,000 and profit rises to USD 1,740,000. What is return on assets if sales hold?
Marketing estimates an inventory cut will cost 1% of sales. The break-even sales loss is 1.70%. What is the right reading of that position?

options.text: The decision rests on a forecast with only 0.7 percentage points of margin
The proposal is safe, since 1% sits below 1.70%
The proposal fails, because the sales at risk exceed the carrying cost released
The break-even figure should be recalculated on a less conservative basis

lessons.title: 6 - Operational Metrics
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: Customers are finding a large share of a plant's defects relative to the share found by quality control. What does that ratio measure?

options.text: The severity of the defects reaching the market
The inspection system, which indicates a detection problem
The reliability of damage frequency reported by functional area
The supplier performance index of incoming material

questions.text: Purchases from a supplier total USD 600,000 and nonconformance costs attributed to it are USD 30,000. Its quoted price is USD 80 per unit. What is the adjusted price for comparison?
You rank a small supplier and a large one on raw supplier performance index values, with the same absolute nonconformance cost. What are you actually measuring?

options.text: The relative quality of the materials each provides
The adjusted price each is charging
Their size, because a smaller purchase total raises the index
The share of nonconformance caused by missing paperwork

questions.text: You benchmark inventory turnover against a competitor. You used cost of goods sold and they used sales. What does the comparison actually reflect?

options.text: The difference in gross margin rather than in inventory management
The dates on which each organisation valued its inventory
Inventory velocity across both organisations
The effect of seasonality on each averaging method

questions.text: A manufacturer's inventory at cost was USD 3,400,000 at the start of the year and USD 2,600,000 at the end. Cost of goods sold was USD 21,000,000. What is inventory turnover?
Which turnover formula suits a trader in commodities whose selling prices move sharply?

options.text: Sales divided by average inventory valued at selling price
Cost of goods sold divided by average inventory at cost
Units of product in both the numerator and the denominator
Sales divided by closing inventory at cost

questions.text: A supplier's sales of a product were USD 12,000,000 at USD 400 per unit, and it reports capacity utilisation of 75%. What is its uncommitted capacity?

options.text: 7,500 units
22,500 units
40,000 units
10,000 units

questions.text: Labour cost in a single warehouse area is well above the other areas. Which second measure tells you which remedy applies?

options.text: Labour hours used in that area, which separates rates from hours
Units shipped per employee across the whole site
Equipment downtime in that area
Orders per salesperson for the same period

lessons.title: 7 - Dashboards and Scorecards
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: A supplier reports 98% delivery performance measured against dates it set itself. What is wrong with the measure, and what is the fix?

options.text: It has no target value, so add a good, better and best band
It is not quantified, so report customers affected instead
It carries a single parameter, so measure against the customer's requested date
It is retrospective, so move it onto a near-real-time feed

questions.text: A dashboard puts performance data directly in front of the people who can act on it. Who is most likely to resist, and why?

options.text: Staff, who fear that individual performance becomes visible
Suppliers, asked to share data at short intervals
Executives, who lose their periodic summary reports
Managers whose role was the round trip of information up and instructions back down

questions.text: A team builds a scorecard rich in customer, process and learning measures and drops the financial perspective as backward-looking. What is the correct response?

options.text: The financial perspective has to stay, and every other measure needs a stated route to the bottom line
Acceptable, since the design was intended to be future-oriented
Acceptable, provided cash-to-cash cycle time sits under business process
This turns it into a custom scorecard, which is better balanced

questions.text: An organisation designs its own scorecard categories rather than using the four standard perspectives. What does it gain and give up?

options.text: It gains balance and gives up cultural fit
It gains fit to its culture and structure, and gives up the guarantee of balance
It gains executive sponsorship and gives up supplier involvement
It gains financial rigour and gives up the customer view

questions.text: A preclearance measure averages 50% against a target of 5%, every month for a year. What is the mature response?

options.text: Escalate and enforce the existing target more firmly
Remove the measure, since it has never been met
Review whether the measure and the target are accurate and achievable
Replace the supplier, since a miss of that size is unacceptable

questions.text: A scorecard shows each metric's goal, the measure used and the actual result for the period. What is missing, and why does it matter?

options.text: The owner, so nobody is accountable for the result
The trend, so the direction of travel is invisible
The data source, so the figure cannot be validated
The target, and without it the number is a fact rather than a measure

questions.text: What distinguishes a dashboard from a scorecard when both carry the same underlying measures?

options.text: Cadence and audience: near-real-time and personal against periodic and shared
Dashboards carry operational measures and scorecards carry financial ones
Dashboards need targets while scorecards need only actuals
Dashboards are internal while scorecards are shared with customers

questions.text: A scorecard is to span several companies in a chain. What has to be established before any reporting structure is designed?

options.text: A common information system across all partners
Agreement at executive level across the chain, since there is no shared authority above
A third-party auditor to police the submitted figures
Penalty clauses in each supply contract

lessons.title: 8 - A Common Process Language
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: NESR adopts a standard process vocabulary for its supply chain instead of describing each site in local terms. What does that buy that internal measures cannot?

options.text: It removes the need for departmental performance measures
It guarantees that the processes themselves are efficient
It lets one organisation's chain be compared with another's on a like-for-like basis
It removes the need for targets, because the definitions are standard

questions.text: Which process family covers establishing and maintaining the information, business rules, contracts and compliance a chain needs in order to operate?

options.text: Enable
Plan
Source
Deliver

questions.text: A pump is returned by a customer and then refurbished for resale. Which process family covers the refurbishment itself?

options.text: Return, because the item came back through the reverse flow
Make, because refurbishment converts the item
Enable, because the work maintains the organisation's assets
Deliver, because the item re-enters the customer order process

questions.text: Why do measures built on process families behave differently from measures built on departments?

options.text: Process measures are cheaper to collect
Departmental measures cannot be quantified
Process measures are always reported in real time
Processes cross the boundaries between functions and companies, so no single function can move the number or claim it

questions.text: Order fulfilment cycle time is the measure that is failing. Which kind of activity should you examine first?

options.text: Planning activities, which balance aggregate demand and supply at intervals
Governance activities, which set business rules and contracts
Execution activities, which are triggered by demand and change the state of goods
Site-specific activities, which each organisation defines for itself

questions.text: A service line sources new materials for each contract, has the longest lead times and a low fill rate. Which order fulfilment approach is it running?

options.text: Engineer-to-order
Make-to-order
Make-to-stock
Configure-to-order

questions.text: Why would a chain deliberately accept below-target performance at one link?

options.text: Because measures at the same level of detail have to be introduced one at a time
Because overall velocity can improve if one link absorbs a penalty, provided the trade-off is negotiated and the reward shared
Because the weakest link sets the target for all the others
Because underperformance at a single link is offset automatically in the aggregate

questions.text: NESR wants to start using chain-level process measures with its partners. Which start is most likely to succeed?

options.text: Publish the full measure set and require monthly returns from every partner
Measure every process family internally for a year before involving partners
Announce the programme at a supplier conference to build momentum
Apply a single measure across 2 or 3 partners and prove it works

lessons.title: 9 - The Five Performance Attributes
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: A service line's 4 gates measure 94%, 97%, 96% and 98% over a quarter. What is the perfect order fulfilment rate?
Gates stand at 94%, 97%, 96% and 98%, and there is money to lift a single gate to 99%. Which choice gives the largest gain?

options.text: The 98% gate, because it is closest to 99% and cheapest to move
The 96% gate, because documentation errors touch every order
The 94% gate, because the gain is the ratio of new to old
Any of them, because a percentage point is worth the same wherever it is taken

questions.text: An order's cycle contains 13.5 days of process time and 6.5 days of dwell. What is the cycle time, and what share of it is dwell?

options.text: 20 days, with dwell at 48%
20 days, with dwell at 32.5%
13.5 days, because dwell sits outside the cycle
7 days, being the difference between process time and dwell

questions.text: The dwell in a 20-day cycle is credit release, waiting for a full load, and time at the customs broker. Where should the improvement effort go?

options.text: The 6 days of sourcing, the largest single element
The 20-day total, since that is what the customer experiences
Reclassify dwell as process time, since the order stays in the system throughout
The 3 dwell items, which need policy decisions rather than investment

questions.text: Inventory days of supply are 78, days sales outstanding 64 and days payables outstanding 52. If inventory days fall to 60, what happens to cash-to-cash cycle time?

options.text: It falls from 90 days to 78 days
It falls from 194 days to 176 days
It falls from 90 days to 72 days
It rises from 90 days to 108 days

questions.text: A finance director asks which measures show how hard the capital tied up in the chain is working. Which set answers that?

options.text: Cash-to-cash cycle time, return on fixed assets and return on working capital
Perfect order fulfilment and order fulfilment cycle time
Upside and downside adaptability, and value at risk
Total cost to serve and cost of goods sold

questions.text: Downside adaptability is the order reduction a chain can absorb at 30 days' notice with no inventory or cost penalty. Which claim fails that test?

options.text: A 20% cut absorbed by rescheduling supplier deliveries inside the notice period
A 20% cut achieved by writing off raw material already committed
A 20% cut absorbed by standing down planned overtime
A 20% cut absorbed by returning unopened material under an agreed clause

questions.text: Supply chain revenue is USD 24,000,000, cost of goods sold USD 15,600,000, supply chain management cost USD 3,600,000 and supply chain fixed assets USD 12,000,000. What is the return on those fixed assets?

lessons.title: 10 - Continuous Improvement and Its Toolkit
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: An improvement programme has produced a set of small local wins that never add up to a strategy. Which of the two directions was reversed?

options.text: Implementation was run from the top by people who do not do the work
Selection was made at the bottom instead of by top management
Benchmarks were set internally rather than against a competitor
The team analysed the process before describing it in depth

questions.text: An organisation cuts spending on inspection, audits, testing and calibration in order to save money. What follows?

options.text: Quality of design falls, since design faults are caught by inspection
Cost of poor quality falls, because fewer nonconformities are recorded
Appraisal cost rises as defects surface later in the process
Cost of poor quality rises, and it includes inefficient processes and lost opportunities

questions.text: A company cut accounts payable headcount by 20% working to its own goal. After comparing itself with an outside organisation, it cut from 500 people to 75. What did the comparison supply?

options.text: A more accurate way to measure accounts payable productivity
A process design that could be copied step by step
The knowledge that an 85% reduction was possible
Justification for presenting the reduction to the board

questions.text: What separates a Pareto chart from a histogram?

options.text: Pareto shows characteristics such as defect type, while a histogram shows a distribution of measurements
Pareto is a non-quantitative tool, while a histogram is quantitative
Pareto plots two variables against each other, while a histogram plots one
Pareto carries control limits at plus and minus 3 sigma

questions.text: Customers complained that the seats in a car were too low, although the seats met specification. Investigation found that lowering the window ledges resolved it. What does the case teach?

options.text: Customers needed instruction on adjusting the seats
The stated complaint was a symptom and the root cause lay elsewhere
The complaints were special cause variation and could be discounted
Enquiry should stop once a complaint is shown to be factually wrong

questions.text: A product conforms perfectly to specification but sells poorly because customers do not value its features. How should that be classified?

options.text: A marketing failure that sits outside the quality system
A conformance failure, since customer requirements were not met
Not a quality issue, because no defects were produced
A failure of quality of design, which process control cannot detect

questions.text: A control chart shows a single reading beyond the upper limit after months of readings inside the limits. What does that call for?

options.text: Redesign of the process, since the variation is inherent
Widening the limits to reflect actual performance
Investigation of that occurrence as a special cause
Recalculating the mean to include the new reading

questions.text: A team knows a picking process is unreliable but not why. Which sequence of tools fits?

options.text: A check sheet to see what is happening, a Pareto chart to see what matters, then cause-and-effect to see why
Cause-and-effect first, then a check sheet to confirm the chosen cause
A scatter chart first, then a histogram of the same data
A control chart first, then a matrix diagram of supplier specifications

lessons.title: 11 - Lean, Waste and Six Sigma
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: A cell has 840 productive minutes a day and demand rises from 120 to 150 assemblies a day. What is the new takt time, and what has to happen?

options.text: 7 minutes, and the cell should run faster to build a buffer
5.6 minutes, and output should exceed takt to protect against demand swings
5.6 minutes, and the cell must be redesigned to the new takt or capacity raised by 25%
6.7 minutes, and capacity must be raised by 20%

questions.text: A cell consistently produces faster than its takt time. How should that be read?

options.text: As overproduction, the most serious of the wastes, quietly building inventory
As a productivity gain that deserves recognition
As evidence that takt was calculated on the wrong demand figure
As acceptable, provided quality is unaffected

questions.text: A cell records 160 defects in a month across 12,000 jobs. The manager redefines opportunities from 1 per job to 4. What happens to the reported rate?

options.text: It rises from 3,333 to 13,333 defects per million opportunities
It is unchanged, since the defect count is unchanged
It rises, because counting more opportunities means more chances to fail
It falls from 13,333 to 3,333 defects per million opportunities

questions.text: A plant scrambles to hit forecast figures at quarter end, stretches its routines, and then suffers downtime, mistakes and waiting. What is the causal order?

options.text: Waste in the process created unevenness, which then overburdened the staff
Uneven demand created overburden, and the overburden produced the waste
Overburden is the root cause and unevenness is one of its effects
The waste came from operators departing from standardised work

lessons.title: 12 - Theory of Constraints and Just-in-Time
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: A constraint workstation completes 60 units an hour. The station feeding it is raised to 65 units an hour. Over an 8-hour shift, what happens?

options.text: Output rises to 520 units
Output stays at 480 units and the following station becomes the constraint
Output stays at 480 units and 40 units of work pile up ahead of the constraint
Output rises to 520 units, with 40 units left in process

questions.text: A lean programme has improved cash flow, yet standard cost reports show profit falling. What is the explanation?

options.text: Traditional measures reward machine utilisation and the absorption of overhead into inventory
Lean moves cost from overhead into direct labour, which is expensed sooner
Setup cost rises as lot sizes fall, offsetting the holding cost saved
Appraisal cost rises while the cost of poor quality falls

questions.text: Why does removing inventory buffers improve quality rather than simply cutting cost?

options.text: Because smaller lots are inspected more thoroughly at each stage
