Because a defective part can no longer be swapped from stock, so it stops the flow and gets investigated
Because suppliers are contractually obliged to ship defect-free goods
Because holding cost falls, releasing budget for quality work

questions.text: A changeover takes 90 minutes. Where does the first and cheapest reduction usually come from?

options.text: Buying quick-release fixtures for the machine
Documenting adjustments to remove trial and error
Increasing lot sizes so that fewer changeovers are needed
Reclassifying tasks so that everything that can be done while the machine runs is moved off the stopped time

lessons.title: 13 - Change Management
lessons.body: Watch the video, then take the knowledge check below. You need 70% to pass, and you can retake it as many times as you like.

questions.text: An initiative has stalled. Staff understand why it matters and have been trained on the tools, but nobody wants it. What is missing, and what fixes it?

options.text: Knowledge, so more communication about the benefits
Skill, so further training on the tools
Knowledge, so a clearer picture of the end state
Desire, which neither training nor communication supplies

questions.text: A programme arrives in the organisation as a finished plan with a budget and a timeline. Why is it likely to fail?

options.text: It skipped the preparation stage, where almost all of the desire is produced
It skipped success criteria, which belong before any planning
Execution delivers knowledge rather than skill, so training is missing
Funding should be secured only after execution has begun

questions.text: A manager argues that consulting staff is pointless because most of their suggestions will not be adopted. What is the answer?

options.text: Correct, so consultation should be limited to those holding decision rights
Being asked genuinely, before the decision is made, still creates buy-in
Correct, unless the suggestions come from directly affected functions
Consultation should follow funding approval, once the plan is fixed

questions.text: Several months into a change programme, objections stop being raised. How should that be read?

options.text: As acceptance, since the earlier fears have been addressed
As a signal to accelerate while support is high
As the same resistance, now invisible
As proof that the vision was championed well by top management

questions.text: An employee raises a fear about a change in a team meeting. You take it seriously and reply to that employee privately. What is wrong with that?

options.text: Nothing, provided the reply is documented
The concern should have been referred to the programme sponsor
Individual fears belong with line managers rather than the programme
The silent people who share the fear never hear the answer

questions.text: A lean programme is being planned. Which function's measurement basis has to change, or the programme will appear to lose money?

options.text: Finance and accounting, which needs measures that show the benefits of the new methods
Marketing, which moves from make-and-sell to sense-and-respond
Purchasing, which moves from lowest cost to relationship building
Distribution, which needs systems to select transport modes on the fly

questions.text: What does recognising the slow pace of cultural change require of a change programme?

options.text: Delay the physical changes until the culture has caught up
Build the cultural effort into ongoing operations rather than running it as a project
Replace cultural objectives with measurable process objectives
Concentrate the cultural work in the final phase, once the systems are stable

questions.text: Side effects of incentives are hard to predict. What follows for a new metric set?

options.text: Choose fewer measures, so that fewer side effects can arise
Let the functions being measured choose their own measures
Use analysis of actual results as feedback and keep revising the measures
Replace the measures with live dashboards, which need no targets

lessons.title: 14 - Wrap-up
lessons.body: A recap of the release, and what it sets you up to do next.
